channel.description: Technical write-ups on machine learning, statistics, linear algebra, and the tooling around them, by Ravi Kalia.

item.title: Stein’s Method, Part 7: Kernel Stein Discrepancy as a Regulariser
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
The kernel Stein discrepancy (KSD) can sit in a training loss and pull a batch of codes toward a chosen distribution, using nothing from that distribution but its score.

Anyone who has trained a variational autoencoder has added a KL term to the loss. Anyone who has trained a self-supervised image encoder has added VICReg’s variance and covariance terms, or something like them, to stop every image mapping to the same vector. Both terms say the same thing, make the codes look like , and both say it partially. The VAE’s KL acts on one image at a time, so it also charges for whatever a code says about its image. VICReg’s terms see only the batch covariance, so a batch arranged as ten tight clusters with identity covariance passes them unchanged.

Part 1 proved Stein’s identity and Part 2 turned it into a normal approximation. Part 3 built the kernel Stein discrepancy: a distance from a sample to a target that needs only the target’s score, and for the score is . Part 4 fitted models with the same operator, Part 5 applied it to Markov chains and Part 6 to neural networks. The JEPA nuisance study used KSD as an anti-collapse term without saying what it does to a batch. This part says what it does, and measures it on CIFAR-10.

An AI agent (Claude) ran the experiments and drafted the text and the interactive chart. Separate passes checked each derivation numerically and each reference against its source.

Three ideas carry the post:

  1. KSD of a batch is a loss. For it has a closed form in the batch’s distances and inner products, costs , and its V-statistic is the squared length of the step SVGD would take from the batch. A batch with zero KSD is one SVGD would not move.
  2. The kernel sets what the regulariser can see. Under the linear kernel , KSD is the moment penalty that VICReg-type terms approximate. A characteristic kernel sees the whole law in principle, but in 64 dimensions a wide kernel is nearly linear in the squared distance, and only a narrow one keeps the extra sight.
  3. What a regulariser should see depends on how the codes are used. A VAE decodes draws from , and there a mixed kernel that sees shape gave the best prior samples of six regularisers on CIFAR-10. A JEPA’s embedding only has to avoid collapse, and there KSD with the IMQ kernel, MMD and SIGReg, which in 64 dimensions see little beyond two moments, gave the best linear probes, while the mixed kernel gave the worst of the regularisers that prevented collapse.

1 Notation

  • : a batch of codes, the latents of a VAE or the embeddings of a JEPA. is the batch mean and its second-moment matrix.
  • : the target. Its score is .
  • : the Langevin Stein operator of Part 1, for a vector field . For it is .
  • : a base kernel, with RKHS ; is the -fold product for vector fields. is its Stein kernel. .
  • Two base kernels recur. IMQ, , as in Part 3. Gaussian, , with bandwidth .
  • : the weight of a regulariser in a loss.

2 Regularisers that target

Every regulariser in this post takes the codes an encoder produces and returns a number that is small when they look like draws from . Six are compared.

  • KL, the VAE’s term. The encoder outputs a mean and variances for each image, and pays per image (Kingma & Welling 2014).
  • Moments. : the batch’s mean and second moments against the target’s. The experiments use an unbiased version of it (Section 3.2).
  • VICReg (Bardes et al. 2022): a hinge on each coordinate’s standard deviation below 1, plus the squared off-diagonal covariances. It names no target distribution and has no term for the mean.
  • MMD (Gretton et al. 2012): compares the batch with a fresh sample through kernel averages.
  • SIGReg (Balestriero & LeCun 2025): projects the batch onto random unit directions and compares each projection’s empirical characteristic function with , the characteristic function of , through an Epps–Pulley-type statistic (Epps & Pulley 1983). This post follows the paper’s Algorithm 1: weight , 17 quadrature points on , the statistic multiplied by the batch size, 256 directions redrawn every step. The paper recommends 1,024 directions.
  • KSD (Liu, Lee & Jordan 2016; Chwialkowski, Strathmann & Gretton 2016): the U-statistic of Part 3,

They differ in what they need from the target:

Regulariser Needs from Acts on Cost per batch
KL its density, and the encoder’s one image at a time
Moments mean and covariance the batch
VICReg a target standard deviation the batch
MMD samples the batch
SIGReg the 1-D characteristic function the batch, along directions
KSD the score the batch

is the number of directions and the number of quadrature points in SIGReg’s integral.

2.1 The VAE’s KL term

The VAE’s term is not a batch regulariser. Averaged over the data, it splits into two parts (Hoffman & Johnson 2016):

ELBO surgery

is the aggregate posterior: the law of a code when the image is drawn at random. Hoffman & Johnson write the mutual information between and the image’s index in the data set, which is the same quantity for a finite data set.

Proof. Split the log-ratio inside the KL through , then average over and :

  • Sampling from the prior needs only the second term to be small. The first term is the price of a code that carries information about its image.
  • A batch regulariser targets the second term alone: the batch of codes is a sample from . That is the Wasserstein autoencoder’s design (Tolstikhin et al. 2018), with MMD as the batch term; InfoVAE’s MMD variant does the same (Zhao et al. 2019).

3 KSD of a batch

Part 3 wrote the Stein kernel for a general target and base kernel. Its four terms pair the score with the kernel and its derivatives:

For every term is explicit.

Proposition 1 — the Stein kernel of N(0, I)

For the Gaussian base kernel with ,

For the IMQ base kernel ,

Proof. For the Gaussian kernel, and . With , the three groups of terms are

Their sum is Equation 2. For the IMQ kernel the same three lines use

and sum to Equation 3.

The colours follow the three groups. The score–score term rewards pairs that point in opposite directions from the origin. The trace term’s charges every pair close enough to share the kernel, which pushes codes apart. The cross terms and the rest of the trace term give back in proportion to the squared distance, and under the three balance to zero on average. Both forms were checked against automatic differentiation of the four-term formula to .

Smallest instance. On the diagonal, , and Equation 2 gives . The V-statistic includes those diagonal terms, the U-statistic does not. So

The V-statistic is the U-statistic plus a ridge penalty of weight on the codes. Section 3.2 says which to train with.

3.1 Relation to SVGD

Part 3’s Theorem 3 (Liu & Wang 2016) found the direction in which moving a sample lowers its KL divergence to fastest:

and Part 3’s Theorem 2 showed . Applied to the batch’s own empirical law:

KSD of a batch is the length of its SVGD step

The bracket, averaged over the batch, is the velocity SVGD would give every point.

  • A batch with zero V-statistic KSD is a fixed point of SVGD: the drift toward the origin and the repulsion between codes cancel everywhere.
  • Penalising KSD and running SVGD on the codes use the same field. SVGD moves the codes along it, which needs only the score (amortised SVGD; Wang & Liu 2016; Part 4). The KSD penalty differentiates its squared length, which needs the derivative of the score as well. For that derivative is , so the two cost the same.
  • Minimising KSD over a free set of particles, with no encoder, is KSD descent (Korba et al. 2021). It can stall at spurious stationary points, such as configurations symmetric about a plane.

3.2 U- or V-statistic

The two estimators differ by the diagonal, and as losses they fail in opposite directions.

  • The V-statistic is never negative, because Equation 4 writes it as a squared norm. Its expectation over batches is not , though: it adds , which for both base kernels grows with . Minimising it shrinks the codes. The bias carries a factor , so it matters most in high dimension.
  • The U-statistic is unbiased: averaged over batches it equals , which is zero only at . But it can be negative, and for some kernels it has no floor. Under the linear kernel of Section 4, one code sent far out lowers it without limit whenever the rest of the batch is slightly narrower than the target along that code’s direction, at a rate proportional to . Under IMQ, two codes sent off in opposite directions lower it more slowly, since Equation 3 gives for large . Under the Gaussian kernel every term decays, so it is bounded.

The rule this post follows:

  • Descending a fixed set of points, as in the interactive chart of Section 4.1, needs a loss with a floor: the V-statistic.
  • Training an encoder on fresh batches needs the right expectation: the U-statistic. Its escape routes are not hypothetical. The VAE of Section 6 found both at strong , so a U-statistic loss needs a kernel whose Stein kernel is bounded, or a watch on the largest codes.

3.3 Gradient of the moment penalty

The moment penalty’s gradient on one code is

It is an affine function of , with the same matrix for every code. A gradient step therefore moves the whole batch by one affine map, and an affine map sends a ring to an ellipse and four clusters to four clusters. Whatever shape the batch has beyond its first two moments, this penalty can stretch it but never change it. KSD’s gradient on depends on where the other codes are, so it can.

That holds for as written, the V-statistic the chart descends. The U-statistic the experiments train on (Section 3.2) adds a self-term,

which is not affine. For , descent along it pushes each code outward along its own direction, harder the farther out the code already is. That is the escape route the CIFAR-10 runs found.

4 Kernel choice

The moment penalty is not a different kind of object from KSD. It is KSD under the simplest kernel.

Proposition 2 — the moment penalty is KSD under the linear kernel

Let and . For every with finite second moments, with and ,

Applied to the batch’s empirical law, this is .

Proof. The RKHS of is the affine functions with norm . So is the affine vector fields , with .

  1. For such , , so .
  2. Taking expectations, .
  3. KSD is the supremum of over . A linear functional’s supremum over a unit ball is the norm of its representer, here , whose squared norm is Equation 5.
  • Reading. The linear kernel tests Stein’s identity on affine vector fields only. A constant field checks the mean and a linear field checks the second moments; nothing in the test class can see a third moment.
  • VICReg depends on the batch only through its covariance matrix, so it is blind to the same things, and to the mean as well.
  • Polynomial kernels. Under the test fields are polynomials of degree , and is a polynomial of degree : KSD then sees moments up to order .
  • Characteristic kernels. Under the IMQ or Gaussian kernel, only when (Liu, Lee & Jordan 2016; Chwialkowski, Strathmann & Gretton 2016). Gorham & Mackey (2017) add that the IMQ KSD also controls convergence, while for the Gaussian KSD can go to zero along a sequence whose mass escapes to infinity.

4.1 Two-dimensional batches

The chart puts the comparison where it can be seen. It draws a batch of codes in two dimensions, from a law with the same mean and covariance as , and the direction each regulariser would move every code. Its bars score the batch under all five regularisers, in standard deviations above their spread on Gaussian batches of the same size. Descending moves the codes themselves, with no encoder in between, using the V-statistic (Section 3.2).

Things to try. The ranges are over the first five draws (“New draw”) at the default batch size of 150.

  1. Ring, Moments. The arrows are short, and the Moments bar sits between −1.0 and 0.8 null standard deviations, inside the tick. Every kernel bar is far past it: KSD with the IMQ kernel at 23–29, the Gaussian kernel at 49–56, MMD at 6–12, SIGReg at 9–13.
  2. Press Descend. After the full 3,000 steps the mean of is still 4.1–4.2, against 8 for , and the mean of is still 2.00. The moment penalty has nothing to correct, so the ring stays a ring (Section 3.3).
  3. Switch to KSD IMQ, press New draw, then Descend. The ring fills in: the mean of ends at 6.6–6.7. The mean of ends at 1.92, below 2. That is the V-statistic’s ridge penalty from Section 3.2, pulling codes in. With the Gaussian kernel it ends at 1.81–1.82.
  4. Shrunk. Every regulariser flags a batch with the wrong scale, the moment penalty included (56–60 null standard deviations). Collapse is a failure of the second moment, which every regulariser here can see.

4.2 High dimension

The chart is two-dimensional. The CIFAR-10 runs use , and there a characteristic kernel can see much less than it can in principle.

The reason is concentration. For two independent draws , is : its mean is and its standard deviation , a relative spread of , or 18% at . Expand the base kernel around :

  • The affine part depends on and only through , and : a kernel of low polynomial degree, close kin of the linear kernel. El Karoui (2010) proves the matrix version: for data with independent coordinates, as the sample size and dimension grow together, a kernel matrix is close to a linear-kernel matrix plus low-rank terms.
  • What is left for seeing shape is the curvature. Its size relative to the slope, one standard deviation of away from , is

Base kernel at
IMQ,
Gaussian, (the usual MMD median heuristic)
Gaussian, , (the SVGD median heuristic)

The first two kernels are close to affine in over every pair a batch contains, so their KSD sees about what the moment penalty sees. Only the narrow Gaussian kernel keeps enough curvature to see shape. This is one face of the decline in power of kernel tests with dimension at a fixed sample size, against alternatives that do not get easier as the dimension grows (Ramdas et al. 2015). Zhao et al. (2019) report the same from the training side: their VAE regularised with the SVGD direction performed well only with a two-dimensional latent space.

A direct test makes the point. Four laws share the target’s mean and covariance: the corners of the cube , the sphere of radius , independent coordinates with Student- tails scaled to variance 1, and ten Gaussian clusters, whitened. For each law and each regulariser, 200 batches of were drawn; a batch is flagged when its value exceeds the 95th percentile of the same regulariser on 200 Gaussian batches. A regulariser that sees only the first two moments flags about 5% of batches. The control column runs 200 fresh Gaussian batches against the same threshold: its spread around 5% is the noise in every other cell.

Regulariser , all four : control corners sphere clusters
Moments 0%–11.5% 9.5% 2% 8.5% 11.5% 6.5%
KSD, IMQ 40.5%–100% 4% 4.5% 4% 7% 7%
KSD, Gaussian, 56.5%–100% 4% 4.5% 4% 8% 8%
KSD, Gaussian, 73%–100% 6% 12% 8% 33% 99.5%
KSD, mixed 56.5%–100% 6.5% 9.5% 8.5% 19.5% 80.5%
MMD, WAE kernel 21.5%–100% 4.5% 7% 3.5% 5% 4.5%
SIGReg 38%–100% 6% 11.5% 12% 10% 7.5%

The column ranges over the four laws; for every kernel the lowest figure is the law, and the control there is 1–6%. One threshold per dimension, from one seed. The mixed kernel is defined in Section 4.3; SIGReg uses 256 directions.

  • In two dimensions every characteristic kernel flags the corners, the sphere and the clusters every time, and the heavy tails 21.5–73% of the time. The moment penalty flags 0–6% of the three light-tailed laws and 11.5% of the heavy-tailed one: its own estimate spreads with the fourth moment, which is how heavy tails reach it.
  • In 64 dimensions IMQ, the wide Gaussian kernel and MMD stay within a few points of their controls: from one batch they see about what the moment penalty sees. Only the narrow kernels pick up the clusters.
  • SIGReg looks at one-dimensional projections, and most projections of a high-dimensional law are close to Gaussian (Diaconis & Freedman 1984). The clusters occupy 9 of the 64 dimensions, and most of its 256 random directions point mostly elsewhere.

4.3 Scale control

The narrow kernel has the opposite problem. A Gaussian kernel at a fixed bandwidth sees nothing of a batch whose codes are far apart compared with , and its KSD falls toward zero as the batch spreads. This is Gorham & Mackey’s (2017) warning about Gaussian-kernel KSD, that it ignores mass in the tails, here acting on a loss.

A test separates the two failure modes. An encoder in miniature produces , with redrawn every step, and learns only the 64 scales and the shift , by Adam on the regulariser alone. The right answer is every . The scales start log-uniform on , and three seeds were run for 1,500 steps each.

Loss on fresh batches of 256 Learned scales, three seeds (target 1)
Moments, V-statistic 0.85–0.93
Moments, U-statistic 0.95–1.05
KSD, IMQ, V-statistic 0.63–0.75
KSD, IMQ, U-statistic 0.91–1.09
KSD, Gaussian, , U-statistic 0.16–9.07
KSD, mixed kernel, U-statistic 0.94–1.06
MMD, WAE kernel 0.91–1.09
SIGReg 0.89–1.11
  • The V-statistics shrink every coordinate: by up to 15% for the moment penalty and by 25–37% for IMQ. That is the ridge penalty of Section 3.2, scaled up by .
  • The narrow Gaussian kernel on its own does not recover the scale at all.

The fix uses the linearity of KSD in its base kernel: the Stein kernel of is , so

The mixed kernel of this post is IMQ plus times a Gaussian kernel. IMQ’s heavy tails pin the scale and the Gaussian part sees the shape. Its bandwidth is set from the batch, with the median squared distance between codes, as in SVGD. Under the target , which gives the of the detection table. The gradient flows through the median. With the median detached, spreading the batch lowers the loss at the current bandwidth. The descent direction then points outward even when the batch is already too wide (in a test at , at 1.5, 3 and 10 times the target’s scale), so nothing stops it spreading. The weight is the ratio of the two parts’ standard deviations on Gaussian batches, rounded: it lets the Gaussian part’s signal through without drowning it in IMQ’s noise.

5 Data: CIFAR-10

The two experiments ask a regulariser for different things. A VAE samples from the prior, so every part of the code distribution the decoder never saw becomes a bad image. A JEPA never samples: its embedding is used through linear probes and nearest neighbours, so it only has to avoid collapse.

  • Source. CIFAR-10 (Krizhevsky 2009): 60,000 colour images of 32 × 32 pixels in ten classes (airplane, automobile, bird, cat, deer, dog, frog, horse, ship, truck), 6,000 per class, split 50,000 for training and 10,000 for test. The images come from the 80 million tiny images collection, and paid students labelled them.
  • Motive. It was built as a benchmark for object recognition at small scale.
  • What this post asks of it. Whether decoded draws from look like its images, and whether a self-supervised embedding separates its classes.
  • Cost of a wrong answer. Choosing a regulariser that costs reconstruction quality and buys nothing, or one that leaves the codes off the target where the decoder has never been trained.
  • Why it fits. Natural images with known classes give both a generative test and a representation test, at a size where the more than a hundred training runs behind this post fit on one laptop GPU (an Apple M1 Pro).

6 A VAE on CIFAR-10

6.1 Setup

  • Encoder. Three convolutions with stride 2 (64, 128 and 256 channels, batch norm, SiLU), then a linear map to codes. The VAE’s encoder outputs 128 numbers, a mean and a log-variance per coordinate.
  • Decoder. The mirror image, with transposed convolutions and a sigmoid output.
  • Loss. The squared reconstruction error summed over an image’s 3,072 pixels, averaged over the batch, plus .
    • KL arm: the standard VAE. The code is sampled, , and is the per-image KL.
    • Batch arms: the encoder is deterministic and acts on the batch of 256 codes: moments, MMD, SIGReg, KSD with IMQ, KSD with the mixed kernel. With MMD this is the Wasserstein autoencoder of Tolstikhin et al. (2018).
    • All KSD and moment terms are U-statistics (Section 3.2).
  • Training. 15 epochs of Adam (learning rate , cosine schedule), batch 256, two seeds per setting, four values of per regulariser, and a plain autoencoder for reference.

6.2 Measurements

  • Reconstruction: mean squared error per pixel on the 10,000 test images.
  • Prior samples: 10,000 codes drawn from and decoded. Their quality is the Fréchet distance between Gaussians fitted to classifier features of the decoded images and of the test images, . This is the FID formula of Heusel et al. (2017) with a different feature map: a small convolutional classifier trained once on CIFAR-10 (92.3% test accuracy) in place of an ImageNet Inception network. Its numbers compare runs within this post and nowhere else.
  • Reconstructions get the same distance, as a floor: the decoder’s own blur, before any mismatch between codes and prior. The gap between the two distances is what the regulariser can close.
  • The codes themselves, for the test images (for the VAE, its samples ): , and the mean squared 2-Wasserstein distance between and the codes projected onto 512 random directions.

6.3 Results

The figure plots each regulariser’s trade-off: reconstruction error against the quality of decoded prior samples, one point per strength .

  • Every regulariser earns its place. The plain autoencoder reconstructs best (mean squared error per pixel), but its decoded prior samples score 9.74 against 5.09 for its reconstructions: its codes are nowhere near ().
  • The mixed kernel gives the best prior samples at every strength above the weakest. At it reaches 5.70 (5.60–5.79 over the two seeds) at reconstruction error . At comparable reconstruction error the others score 6.46–6.69: moments 6.46 at 8.43, KSD with IMQ 6.54 at 9.49, SIGReg 6.64 at 8.47, MMD 6.69 at 8.40, KL 6.69 at 9.04. No other regulariser gets below 6.15 at any strength tried.
  • The gap between prior samples and reconstructions is the part a regulariser can close. The mixed kernel leaves 0.37–0.47 of it at ; every other batch regulariser leaves at least 0.58.
  • KL closes the gap the other way. At its gap is only 0.19, and its codes have the smallest sliced 2-Wasserstein distance to of any run (0.0005). But its reconstructions score 6.58: the per-image KL charges for the information in the code (Equation 1), and the decoder blurs.
  • The two U-statistics without a floor were exploited, as Section 3.2 warned. Among the first 2,000 test codes, the largest draw from would have norm about 10, and the ten largest would carry about 0.8% of the total squared norm.
    • Moment penalty, (six runs): the largest code has norm 23–136. At the ten largest carry 15–21%, and the mean excess kurtosis of the projections is 30.
    • KSD with IMQ, (four runs): largest norm 31–58, the ten largest 4–10%.
    • Every other regularised run, the mixed kernel’s included: largest norm at most 19.2, the ten largest at most 2.1%.
  • The code diagnostics do not explain the mixed kernel’s lead. MMD, SIGReg and the mixed kernel all bring the codes’ covariance within about 0.2 of and their projections within a sliced 2-Wasserstein distance of 0.002 of . Whatever the mixed kernel fixes beyond that lives where second moments and one-dimensional projections cannot see, and the detection table found only the narrow kernels looking there.

The decoded samples themselves, at reconstruction errors between and :

Every row is blurred, as small autoencoders on CIFAR-10 are. The differences the Fréchet distance measures show as saturation and contrast. The moment penalty’s row is oversaturated, the KL row washed out, and the mixed kernel’s row the most varied in colour and contrast.

7 A JEPA on CIFAR-10

A joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA; Assran et al. 2023) learns from two views of one image: an encoder embeds both, and a predictor maps one embedding to the other. Its loss has a trivial minimum, every image sent to the same vector, and the regulariser is what rules it out.

7.1 Setup

  • Views. Two augmentations of each image, after SimCLR (Chen et al. 2020) but simpler: a random resized crop (20–100% of the area), a horizontal flip, colour jitter with probability 0.8 (brightness, contrast and saturation, each of strength 0.4, in a fixed order; no hue jitter), and grayscale with probability 0.2. No blur.
  • Encoder. A small residual network (four residual blocks, 32 to 256 channels, 1.4 million parameters) gives 256 backbone features; an MLP projector maps them to a 64-dimensional embedding . A second MLP, the predictor, maps one view’s embedding to a guess at the other’s.
  • Loss. The mean squared prediction error in both directions plus . There is no EMA target and no stop-gradient, so the regulariser alone prevents collapse, as in the JEPA nuisance study.
  • Arms. VICReg (variance and covariance terms in their published 25 : 1 ratio; since the loss averages the two views’ terms, gives VICReg’s published weights relative to the prediction error), moments, MMD, SIGReg (256 random directions per step), KSD with IMQ, KSD with the mixed kernel, and no regulariser.
  • Choosing . Each arm ran at for 4 epochs with one seed; the value with the best linear-probe accuracy on 5,000 training images held out from the probe was kept. The test set played no part. The chosen values: 0.1 for KSD with IMQ, 1 for MMD and VICReg, and 0.01 for SIGReg, moments and the mixed kernel. SIGReg and moments peaked at the bottom of the grid; the mixed kernel scored between 43.5% and 44.9% at all four values.
  • Training. 12 epochs of AdamW (one-cycle schedule, peak learning rate ), batch 256, three fresh seeds per arm (one for the unregularised run).

7.2 Measurements

  • Linear probe: a logistic regression on the frozen backbone features of the 50,000 training images, scored on the 10,000 test images; and a 20-nearest-neighbour classifier on the same features.
  • The embedding: its class separation, defined with the results, and the same Gaussian diagnostics as the VAE’s codes.

7.3 Results

Test accuracy of the linear probe and the 20-nearest-neighbour classifier, at each arm’s chosen , with the range over three seeds. Class separation is the between-class sum of squares of the embeddings over the within-class sum: how much of the embedding’s spread lies between CIFAR-10’s classes rather than inside them. It and the largest norms quoted below use the first 2,000 test embeddings, stored at half precision. Distance to is the sliced 2-Wasserstein distance of Section 6’s diagnostics, on all 10,000.

Regulariser Linear probe 20-NN Class separation Distance to
KSD, IMQ 0.1 69.3% (68.9–69.5) 65.5% 0.25 0.26
MMD, WAE kernel 1 68.9% (68.7–69.2) 64.5% 0.37 0.05
SIGReg 0.01 67.6% (67.5–67.8) 62.3% 0.40 0.06
VICReg 1 65.6% (64.7–66.4) 60.9% 0.21 0.21
Moments 0.01 56.6% (49.3–60.4) 52.7% 0.03 1.14
KSD, mixed 0.01 44.5% (43.5–45.2) 39.6% 0.08 0.49
None (one seed) — 30.3% 30.9% 0.01 collapsed
  • KSD with IMQ, MMD and SIGReg lead. The first two are level within their seed ranges, and SIGReg is under two points behind. In 64 dimensions all three see little beyond the first two moments of a batch (Section 4.2), and at the chosen strengths none of them makes the embedding Gaussian: its covariance stays 0.9–2.1 away from in .
  • Seeing two moments is not enough on its own. VICReg, which sees only the covariance, is nearly four points behind the leaders (65.6%, at half its published weights, the strength the pilot chose). The moment penalty, which sees exactly the first two moments, does worse still, because the encoder found its escape route again: the largest of its first 2,000 test embeddings has norm 111–238, depending on the seed, the mean excess kurtosis of its projections is 239, and its probe varies by 11 points across seeds.
  • The mixed kernel, best in the VAE, is the worst here of the regularisers that prevent collapse. Its probe reaches 44.5%, and in the pilot it scored 43.5–44.9% at every strength tried. It is not closer to than the leaders: at the prediction loss shrinks its embedding to a third of the target’s scale. But shrinkage does not explain the probe. In the pilot at the same , KSD with IMQ shrank the embedding just as much (mean norm 2.6 against 2.5, distance to 0.49 against 0.48) and kept a class separation of 0.34, against 0.07 for the mixed kernel. The only difference between the two losses is the narrow Gaussian part, the part that sees clusters, and an embedding’s clusters here are its classes.
  • Stronger regularisation removes class structure in every arm. In the pilot, raising from its smallest working value to 10 moved every arm’s embedding toward and cut its class separation: from 0.34 to 0.05 for IMQ, from 0.73 to 0.10 for MMD, from 0.33 to 0.04 for SIGReg. The probe followed once passed each arm’s best value. The mixed kernel starts where the others end.
  • Without a regulariser the embedding collapses. The prediction error reaches zero, every one of the first 2,000 test embeddings lies within 0.2 of the origin, and the probe on the backbone features falls to 30.3%.

The two experiments point in opposite directions, and for the same reason. A VAE decodes draws from the prior, so every region of the code distribution matters and a regulariser that sees shape pays for itself. A JEPA’s embedding is read by a linear probe, which needs the classes apart and the coordinates in use, not a Gaussian. There the three leaders see little beyond two moments, and the one regulariser that sees more flattened the structure the probe needs.

8 Using KSD as a regulariser

The steps the experiments support, for a target whose score is known:

  1. Write the Stein kernel in closed form. For it is Equation 2 or Equation 3. The loss costs per batch and needs the derivative of the score through automatic differentiation; for that derivative is the constant .
  2. Train on the U-statistic. The V-statistic shrinks the codes, by 25–37% per coordinate with IMQ at (Section 4.3).
  3. Choose the kernel by how the codes are used. If they will be sampled, as in a VAE, combine two kernels in high dimension: IMQ alone pins the scale and sees little else, a narrow Gaussian kernel alone sees shape and loses the scale, and the mixed kernel adds them (IMQ plus a Gaussian kernel at the batch’s median bandwidth, gradient through the median, weighted by the ratio of the two parts’ spreads on Gaussian batches). If the regulariser only has to prevent collapse, as in a JEPA, IMQ alone at a small did best here, and the mixed kernel did worst.
  4. Watch the largest codes. A U-statistic whose Stein kernel is unbounded below can be lowered by a few codes sent far out, and an encoder finds that route (Section 6).
  5. Sweep and plot the trade-off. One strength per regulariser compares nothing; Figure 1 needed four per line.

9 Constraints

  • Toy scale. Small networks, 15 and 12 epochs, two or three seeds per setting. The absolute numbers are far from the state of the art on CIFAR-10, and the Fréchet distances use this post’s own classifier, so they compare runs here and nowhere else.
  • One dimension, one batch size. Every run uses and . The curvature argument of Section 4.2 predicts that the balance between wide and narrow kernels moves with both.
  • Coarse frontiers. Four strengths per regulariser, placed using a 3-epoch pilot.
  • Who was tuned. The mixed kernel’s weight and bandwidth come from the synthetic tests of Section 4.2 and Section 4.3, not from CIFAR-10. MMD uses the Wasserstein autoencoder’s published kernel and SIGReg its published Algorithm 1, neither tuned further. A kernel tuned for MMD or more directions for SIGReg might close some of the gap.
  • Other Stein-based fixes untested. Sliced KSD (Gong et al. 2021) optimises its projection directions and is another answer to the blindness of Section 4.2. Pu et al. (2017) train a VAE’s encoder with SVGD itself. Neither was run.
  • The median bandwidth is a piecewise-smooth function of the batch, and its gradient flows through one pair of codes per step.
  • The JEPA’s strengths came from a coarse grid. SIGReg and the moment penalty peaked at its lowest value, 0.01, so a smaller might suit them better. The probe measures linear separability only; the JEPA nuisance study measures what an embedding keeps that it should not, which can rank regularisers differently.

Wide. Kernels. Count. Moments. Narrow. Kernels. See. Shape. Uses. Decide.

item.title: Stein’s Method, Part 6: Neural Networks and Machine Learning
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
Stein’s lemma puts numbers on two facts about neural networks that are usually stated without them: how far a random network of finite width is from its Gaussian-process limit, and which directions in the input a network’s first gradient step can find.

Two statements about neural networks get quoted without a size attached. A randomly initialised network becomes a Gaussian process as its width grows, but nothing in that limit says whether 100 hidden units are close or far. Gradient descent learns features of the input, but nothing in that slogan says which features a single step can see. Both questions are about expectations of functions of Gaussian variables, which is the setting Part 1’s identity was built for. A random network’s output is a sum over hidden units, and Part 2 bounded how far a sum is from the normal. A network’s gradient at initialisation is an average of the label times a function of a Gaussian input, and Part 1 turned such averages into averages of derivatives.

Part 1 proved Stein’s identity and Gaussian integration by parts. Part 2 turned it into a Wasserstein bound for sums. Part 3 and Part 4 used the Langevin operator for sampling and model fitting, and Part 5 for Markov chains. Part 7 puts the kernel Stein discrepancy into training losses.

An AI agent (Claude) drafted the text and the interactive charts. Separate review passes checked each derivation numerically and each reference against its source.

Two ideas carry the post:

  1. A random network is a Gaussian scale mixture. With Gaussian output weights, the output at one input is exactly normal once the hidden layer is fixed, with a random variance . Stein’s lemma applied conditionally bounds the Wasserstein distance from by a constant times , which is of order in the width : an order better than Part 2’s .
  2. Stein’s lemma reads derivatives off data. Under Gaussian inputs, and are the average gradient and average Hessian of the regression function. For a target that depends on one hidden direction, they point along it exactly when the link’s first or second Hermite coefficient is nonzero, and a network’s first gradient step from zero computes the first of them.

A closing section maps where the earlier parts’ tools appear in machine learning.

  • : the width of a hidden layer. : the input dimension.
  • : the Wasserstein-1 distance of Part 2. is the supremum of over with .

Take a network with one hidden layer of width , evaluated at a single input with :

2.3 Rate and constant

The constant can be found too. Expanding to second order in :

The first-order term vanishes because , and gives the closed form. Equation 2’s constant is 8.5 times the true : Proposition 1 gets the order and the dependence on right, and loses a constant factor in the Taylor step.

2.4 Deeper networks

Given the last hidden layer, a deep network’s output is again exactly , so Proposition 1 applies unchanged. What changes is : its terms share the earlier layers, so they are dependent, and equals the limiting variance only up to . Favaro, Hanin, Marinucci, Nourdin & Peccati (2025) prove that one output of a network of any fixed depth, with Gaussian weights and biases, is within of a Gaussian in both Wasserstein and total-variation distance, with lower bounds of the same order against a Gaussian of the same variance. Their key step is Proposition 1’s: Gaussian integration by parts given the previous layer. Balasubramanian, Goldstein, Ross & Salim (2024) use Stein’s method for the whole random field on the input sphere, at a slower rate in width.

2.5 Random networks of five activations

The networks are simulated from their initialisation distribution, not trained: the chart samples 4,000 independent networks of the chosen width and evaluates each at one input. Nothing else is involved. A wrong answer here would be treating a finite network as a Gaussian process, for a prior or a kernel, at a width where it is not one.

The chart shows a histogram of the 4,000 outputs with the exact density, and the exact distance from against width with both bounds. The exact laws come from the representation : is for the linear network, a binomial mixture of laws for ReLU, and a numerical convolution for GELU and tanh.

Things to try:

  1. Defaults (ReLU, ). The histogram is too peaked, with heavier tails than . The exact distance is 0.0861, Part 2’s bound 2.21 and Equation 2’s 0.564.
  2. Width. Drag to 1000. The exact distance is 0.000943, so , against the limit . Part 2’s bound is 0.221, 234 times too large, and Equation 2’s is 0.00798, 8.5 times. From on, the exact curve falls a factor of ten per decade of width, parallel to Equation 2 and steeper than Theorem 4.
  3. One unit. Set . Half of ReLU’s units are inactive at any input, so with one unit the output is exactly 0 with probability 0.5, an atom the chart draws as a spike. At the atom has mass 0.25, at 0.031.
  4. tanh. Its is 0.627, eight times smaller than ReLU’s. At the distance is 0.0122, against 0.0861 for ReLU. A bounded activation fluctuates less in square.
  5. sign. The distance is 0 at every width, because . Part 2’s bound still reads 0.942 at : it sees only the moments of each term, not the conditional Gaussianity.
  6. GELU. , the largest of the five, and at the distance is 0.102.

2.6 Kernels of the limit

The infinite-width limit is a Gaussian process, fixed by its covariance between two inputs. Take with and . Then is standard bivariate normal with correlation , and the limit has covariance

3 Hidden directions

A linear probe, or logistic regression, fits a linear model to data that are not linear, and the fitted coefficients often still point the right way. Stein’s lemma says when and why.

Proposition 3 — average derivatives

Let have a positive, continuously differentiable density on with score , and let for a continuously differentiable . Assume , and are finite. Then

For , , so .

Proof. By the tower property, . For each coordinate , the field satisfies the conditions of Part 3’s Proposition 1, which gives .

The left side is a property of the unknown regression function; the right side is an average over data. When the input density is unknown, has to be estimated first.

3.1 Single-index models

Suppose depends on through one direction only: with , a single-index model. With Gaussian inputs, Equation 3 and one more application of Stein’s lemma give the first two moments:

  • First moment. , and .
  • Second moment. Apply Stein’s lemma to in coordinate : , and .
  • Least squares. With , ordinary least squares converges to . It recovers the direction of a model it does not fit, up to the scale (Brillinger 1983). Li & Duan (1989) extend this beyond Gaussian inputs.
  • Principal Hessian directions. The eigenvectors of estimate the directions of the average Hessian (Li 1992, subtitled “another application of Stein’s lemma”).

Iterating the lemma times, with , gives : the coefficient of in the link’s Hermite expansion is . For a link with a kink, such as ReLU or , read as , since is then a point mass. The first with is the link’s information exponent (Ben Arous, Gheissari & Jagannath 2021). For links standardised to mean 0 and variance 1:

  • Odd links have and even links , so each moment estimator is blind to one family.
  • Information exponent 3, as for , defeats both: the first nonzero moment is a third-order tensor, in the multivariate Hermite basis. Ben Arous et al. (2021) show that online SGD from a random start then needs a number of samples growing like , up to logarithmic factors, for information exponent , against for .

3.2 One gradient step

Train on squared loss, with the first-layer weights started at zero. At , is the constant , so , and the gradient of in is

One step of gradient descent moves every hidden unit along . With samples it moves them along , the first-order Stein estimate. When the step moves the units along noise, and the direction can only enter through higher-order terms: from a small random start , the next term of brings in , the second moment of Equation 4 acting on (for centred ). Ba et al. (2022) show that one gradient step from a random start adds a rank-one spike along the target direction to the first-layer weights, with a size set by the linear (first Hermite) components of the target and the activation. Damian, Lee & Soltanolkotabi (2022) remove the linear part of first; their first step is then driven by the second-order term and recovers the subspace the target depends on.

3.3 Two estimators on synthetic data

The data are synthetic. Inputs are , the hidden direction is a fixed unit vector , and is the link , standardised to mean 0 and variance 1, plus noise. The setting stands in for a regression whose target depends on one unknown combination of many features, the simplest case of feature learning. A wrong answer is a probe that reports no linear signal in a feature that the target depends on.

The chart shows the link’s Hermite coefficients and, against sample size, the overlap between and two estimates: the first-order , and the top eigenvector (largest absolute eigenvalue) of . Lines are means over six data sets and bands their range.

Things to try:

  1. Defaults (ReLU, , , ). Both coefficients are nonzero, and both estimates find : overlaps 0.96 and 0.88. Over 30 data sets the first-order estimate passes 0.9 at and the second-order one at .
  2. tanh. . The first-order overlap reaches 0.99 by . The second-order one stays between 0.27 and 0.37 at every from 25 to 12,800, averaged over 30 data sets; in the chart it wanders between about 0.24 and 0.43 and never rises. Its population matrix is zero, so it estimates noise.
  3. or . Now . The roles swap: the second-order overlap reaches 0.98 to 0.99 by , and the first-order one, averaged over 30 data sets, stays between 0.20 and 0.33 at every (the chart’s six data sets dip to 0.16).
  4. Dimension. For ReLU, averaged over 30 data sets, the at which the first-order overlap passes 0.9 is 100, 200 and 400 at , 20 and 40, and for the second-order estimate 400, 800 and 1600. Both scale linearly in , with the second order needing four times as many samples.
  5. Noise. Over the slider’s range, label noise adds no more error than the randomness of itself; at the two contribute equally. For ReLU at and , averaged over 30 data sets, the first-order overlap is 0.90 at and 0.82 at . The chart’s first six data sets read 0.89 and 0.85.
  6. The floor. A blind estimate need not sit at , the dashed line, which is the root-mean-square overlap of a uniformly random direction. For the linear link at the second-order overlap, averaged over 30 data sets, levels off between 0.46 and 0.55 from on (the chart reads 0.44 to 0.56), against . Its noise is not isotropic: with and , the off-diagonal entries in the row and column of are times noisier than the rest, and the diagonal entry at is times noisier than the other diagonal entries, so even a zero-mean estimate leans toward . It never approaches 1.

4 The series in machine learning

Each tool in the series has an established use in machine learning. Each row names the part that derives the tool and cites a paper that introduced or analysed the use; the two rows about this part point to its sections.

Part Tool Use in machine learning
1 Gaussian integration by parts The gradient of a Gaussian-smoothed objective is an average of function values, for : the evolution-strategies estimator used to train neural-network policies without backpropagation (Salimans et al. 2017). Part 4 gave the score-function and reparameterisation version for policy gradients.
1, 4 SURE Training denoisers without clean data (Soltanayev & Chun 2018, in Part 4). Its Bayesian counterpart, Tweedie’s formula for with marginal density , links denoising to the score (Efron 2011).
2, 6 Normal approximation Width corrections to the Gaussian-process limit of random networks (Section 2).
3 Kernel Stein discrepancy Goodness-of-fit tests against an unnormalised model (Liu, Lee & Jordan 2016; Chwialkowski, Strathmann & Gretton 2016) and sample-quality checks; the anti-collapse regulariser of Nuisance Leakage in JEPA Embeddings, and a training regulariser in general (Part 7).
3 SVGD Posterior inference for Bayesian neural networks (Liu & Wang 2016), policy exploration (Liu et al. 2017), and ensembles with a kernel repulsion between members (D’Angelo & Fortuin 2021).
4 Score matching Denoising score matching (Vincent 2011), the training objective of score-based diffusion models (Song & Ermon 2019).
5 Poisson equation The bias and fluctuations of stochastic-gradient Langevin dynamics (Teh, Thiery & Vollmer 2016), and zero-variance control variates for posterior expectations (Mira, Solgi & Imparato 2013).
6 Hermite coefficients Which directions gradient descent can learn, and how many samples it needs (Section 3).

5 Constraints

  • One input, one hidden layer. Corollary 2 is for one output at one input of a one-hidden-layer network. Two inputs need a multivariate normal approximation, and deeper networks need control of the dependent terms in , which the cited papers supply.
  • Gaussian output weights. With Rademacher output weights the output is not a Gaussian scale mixture, and Proposition 1 does not apply. Part 2’s Theorem 4 still does.
  • Constants. Equation 2 is 8.5 times the true large-width distance for every activation. The rate and the dependence on are right; the factor is lost in the Taylor step of Proposition 1.
  • Gaussian inputs. Equation 4 needs Gaussian . Other input laws need the score in Equation 3, which has to be known or estimated, for example by Part 4’s score matching.
  • Blind spots. Moment estimators of order 1 and 2 cannot see a link of information exponent 3 or more, and their noise floors need not sit at (item 6).
  • One step. Section 3 describes the first gradient step, not training. Later steps change the network’s output, so no longer vanishes.

6 Next in the series

  • Part 7: Part 3’s kernel Stein discrepancy as a training regulariser for the codes of a VAE and the embeddings of a JEPA, and what its kernel lets it see in 64 dimensions.

Widths. Set. Gaussianity. Hermite. Coefficients. Set. Directions. Stein. Measures. Both.

item.title: Stein’s Method, Part 5: Markov Chain Monte Carlo
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
A Markov chain built to sample a density comes with its own Stein operator, and the Stein equation for that operator is the chain’s Poisson equation. One solution of it gives the bias of an approximate sampler such as unadjusted Langevin, the variance of an exact sampler’s averages, and the control variate that would remove that variance.

Every MCMC run fixes a step size and a number of iterations, and both trade accuracy for cost in ways a trace plot does not show. A larger step lowers the autocorrelation. In a sampler without a Metropolis correction it also moves the chain’s long-run distribution away from the target, and no between-chain diagnostic sees that shift, because every chain shifts the same way. Part 3 measured the shift after the run with a kernel Stein discrepancy. Part 2 had a sharper tool in reserve: the Stein equation, whose solution converts a difference of expectations into an expectation under one law. For a Markov chain the same equation sizes the bias and the variance at once.

Part 1 built the Langevin Stein operator. Part 2 solved the Stein equation and noted Barbour’s generator approach in one line; this part runs it. Part 3 audited MCMC output with the kernel Stein discrepancy and built Stein control variates for independent samples. Part 4 fitted unnormalised models. Part 6 turns to neural networks, and Part 7 to training regularisers.

An AI agent (Claude) drafted the text and the interactive charts. Separate review passes checked each derivation numerically and each reference against its source.

Three ideas carry the post:

  1. Markov kernels are Stein operators. If a kernel leaves invariant, for every integrable . The generator of the Langevin diffusion is the Langevin Stein operator applied to gradients, and the Stein equation becomes the Poisson equation.
  2. Bias is a mismatch of operators. An unadjusted sampler’s stationary law satisfies its own kernel’s identity, not the target’s. Evaluating the difference on the Poisson solution gives the bias, first order in the step size for unadjusted Langevin.
  3. Variance comes from the same solution. The Poisson solution sets the asymptotic variance of an exact sampler, and subtracting the generator applied to an approximation of it is a zero-variance control variate.

1 Notation

  • : the target density on , positive and smooth; its score; an unnormalised version.
  • : a Markov chain with transition kernel , acting on functions by .
  • is invariant for if implies .
  • Langevin diffusion: , with a standard Brownian motion. Its generator is .
  • ULA (unadjusted Langevin algorithm): with and step size . Its kernel is and its stationary law .
  • MALA (Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm): the ULA move as a proposal, accepted with the Metropolis–Hastings probability.
  • : a test function; .
  • : the MCMC estimate of .
  • : the asymptotic variance, the limit of .
  • : the solution of the Stein equation, as in Part 2.

2 Markov kernels as Stein operators

Part 1 built a Stein operator by integration by parts. A second construction needs no calculus.

Proposition 1 — a kernel’s Stein identity

2.1 The Langevin generator

In continuous time the kernel becomes a generator, , where moves the diffusion forward by time . By Itô’s formula the Langevin diffusion has generator .

  • Part 2 is the Gaussian case. For the diffusion is the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, . With , the Poisson equation is Part 2’s Stein equation , and Equation 3 is Part 2’s solution with the integrating factor replaced by .

3 The bias of unadjusted Langevin

ULA is the Euler discretisation of the Langevin diffusion. It has no accept step. When it is ergodic its kernel leaves a law invariant, and ; for some targets whose score grows faster than linearly it is not ergodic at all (Roberts & Tweedie 1996). The long-run average converges to , not to . Stein’s method compares the two operators.

Proposition 3 — bias as a mismatch of operators

Let have invariant law , and let solve with and finite. Then

Proof.

  1. Evaluate the Poisson equation under . .
  2. Subtract a zero. Proposition 1 for and gives . Subtract times it.

The structure is Part 2’s. There, became an expectation under of the target’s Stein operator applied to the Stein solution. Here , and the sampler’s law satisfies its own kernel’s identity exactly, so only the difference of the two operators survives.

3.1 First order in the step size

In general has no closed form, but a Taylor expansion in does.

Theorem 4 — first-order bias of ULA in one dimension

Let be positive on with a score that is three times continuously differentiable, and let be such that the Taylor expansion and the integrations by parts in the derivation are justified, with remainders . Then

The order of the bias for smooth goes back to the expansion of Talay & Tubaro (1990) (Durmus & Moulines 2017, Remark 11), and Mattingly, Stuart & Tretyakov (2010) make Poisson-equation arguments of this kind rigorous for time averages of SDE discretisations on the torus. The derivation here is the formal version, checked numerically in Section 3.3.

Three readings:

  • The density. Equation 5 holds for every , so to first order . ULA over-weights wherever is large. For a log-concave target with a Lipschitz score that is the tails, where is large, so ULA’s stationary law is too wide.
  • Smallest instance. For , , and , so the bias in is , the first term of .
  • dimensions. The same expansion gives . For that is , the first-order correction to the Euler–Maruyama invariant density that Leimkuhler, Matthews & Stoltz (2016, Theorem 2.10) derive on the torus. For the bias in is , or per coordinate.

MALA removes the bias. Its accept step makes satisfy detailed balance with , so is invariant and Proposition 3 gives zero. The price is rejections, which can raise the variance at large steps. Within the chart’s range only the two-mode target shows it: at MALA accepts 83% of proposals, and its asymptotic variance for the mean is 1.8 times ULA’s.

3.2 Bias against variance

An average over ULA steps has mean squared error for large .

  • Bias grows like , with from Equation 5.
  • Variance. steps of size cover diffusion time , so , where is the diffusion’s asymptotic variance (Section 4).
  • Optimum. is smallest at . There the mean squared error is , which falls like .

So the root mean squared error of a tuned ULA average falls like , against for an exact sampler. Teh, Thiery & Vollmer (2016) prove the same rate for the mean squared error of stochastic-gradient Langevin dynamics with decreasing step sizes, by a Poisson-equation argument.

3.3 ULA and MALA on three targets

The targets are synthetic one-dimensional densities. Each stands in for a posterior shape:

  • Gaussian: , the large-sample posterior of a regular model. Every quantity has a closed form.
  • Heavier tails: , Gaussian near the centre with exponential tails, like a robust-regression posterior.
  • Two modes: , like a posterior with two explanations of the data.

A wrong answer here means a posterior summary that is off by more than its Monte Carlo error suggests.

The chart computes everything without simulation. Each sampler’s transition kernel is discretised on a grid of 241 points, so its stationary law is a left eigenvector and its asymptotic variance the solution of the discrete Poisson equation (Section 4). Both come from one LU factorisation. A grid of 481 points changes no nonzero bias by more than 0.04%. An independent numpy implementation of the same computation draws Figure 1.

The chart shows ULA’s stationary density minus the target density, and the error of an -step average against step size for both samplers.

Things to try:

  1. Defaults (Gaussian, second moment, , ). ULA’s bias is 0.0526, the exact , and Stein’s first-order prediction is 0.0500. In the left panel ULA’s density minus the target’s is negative at the centre and positive in both tails, so its stationary law is too wide, and the dashed first-order prediction sits almost on it.
  2. Shrink the step. At the bias is 0.00503 against a prediction of 0.00500, a ratio of 1.005. At the ratio is 1.25: the prediction is first order only.
  3. Raise the budget. ULA’s best step, circled on its curve, is 0.148 at , 0.070 at , 0.033 at and 0.016 at . Each tenfold increase in shrinks it by about 2.1 and its error by 2.17 to 2.22, close to . MALA’s best step stays at the slider’s end, 0.4, for every target and estimate, and its error falls by per decade. At the error at each best step is 0.0138 for ULA and 0.00207 for MALA.
  4. Two modes, mean. Stein’s coefficient is . The ratio of exact bias to prediction is 1.033 at , 1.33 at 0.1 and 2.43 at 0.4. Between the modes rises to , where is convex, so the expansion needs a smaller step than on the Gaussian.
  5. Tail probability. On the Gaussian, and . At ULA’s bias is 0.00288, so it reports 0.0257, 13% too high, because is largest in the tails. An indicator is not smooth enough for the derivation of Theorem 4, but the grid confirms its covariance form: the ratio is 1.006 at .
  6. Mean on a symmetric target. On the Gaussian and the heavier-tailed target the bias in the mean is zero at every step, because the target is symmetric and ULA’s step preserves the symmetry. is even, so Stein’s coefficient is zero too. Only the variance term remains, and both samplers’ errors fall as the step grows.

4 The variance of an exact sampler

MALA has no bias, so its error is variance alone. The variance of a Markov chain average is not : neighbouring states are correlated. The Poisson solution measures how much.

Discrete time. For an ergodic chain started at ,

The series , when it converges, solves , and

The chart computes this for both samplers.

Continuous time. For the Langevin diffusion the same quantity has a cleaner form.

Proposition 5 — asymptotic variance from the Poisson solution

Let the Langevin diffusion be started at , let solve , and assume , , and boundary terms that vanish. Then

In one dimension this is : twice the mean square of the Stein solution.

Derivation.

  1. Covariances. The limit is

  2. Integrate the semigroup. , so . The limit is , since .

  3. Integrate by parts. By Equation 2, , so

  • Smallest instance. and : , so the limit is 2. Directly, the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck autocorrelation is , and .
  • Steps of size . steps cover time , so a Langevin-type chain has for small . On the chart’s grid at , Equation 6 is within 1.1% of it for both samplers, every target and every estimate.
  • Slow mixing is a large Stein solution. For the mean, is 2.0 for the Gaussian, 11.7 for the two-mode target and 16.2 for the heavier tails. Part 2 bounded the size of the Stein solution to bound a distance; here its size is the variance.

4.1 Zero-variance control variates

Proposition 2 makes a function with mean zero under for any suitable . Subtracting it from leaves the mean unchanged. With it leaves the constant : an estimate with zero variance. Assaraf & Caffarel (1999) introduced this zero-variance principle in quantum Monte Carlo, and Mira, Solgi & Imparato (2013) brought it to Bayesian MCMC.

Proposition 6 — what a control variate leaves

Under the conditions of Proposition 5 for and for ,

where is the limit in Equation 7.

Proof. , so has mean , and its centred version is . Its Poisson solution is . Apply Proposition 5.

A control variate for MCMC is therefore an approximate solution of the Stein equation, scored by the error in its gradient.

  • Polynomials. Mira et al. take to be a polynomial of degree 1 or 2. Degree 1, , gives : the score itself. Degree 2 adds , so a -dimensional target has control variates.
  • Fitting. Mira et al. fit the coefficients by least squares, as in Part 3’s Proposition 4. These are Part 3’s Stein control variates restricted to gradient fields . Least squares minimises , the variance for independent draws, not Proposition 6’s ; Dellaportas & Kontoyiannis (2012) estimate coefficients aimed at the asymptotic variance instead.
  • Smallest instance. For , . With , the linear has , so exactly. Degree 1 removes all the variance of a Gaussian posterior mean, and degree 2 that of a second moment, since for under .
  • Without the score. Dellaportas & Kontoyiannis (2012) use from Proposition 1 in place of . That needs in closed form, as in many Gibbs samplers, and no score.

4.2 Control variates on a logistic-regression posterior

The data are synthetic: 30 points with features and labels for , seeded, of which 17 are ones. The model is logistic regression with a prior. It stands in for a small study whose posterior mean and tail probability get reported, where a few hundred extra iterations cost little but a wrong second decimal changes a conclusion. The posterior is mildly skewed, so the polynomial control variates are good but not exact.

MALA with step 0.15 samples it, accepting about 76% of proposals. The reference values come from quadrature on a grid: , and . The chart’s score is , and the evidence never appears.

The chart shows the posterior with one chain’s recent states, and that chain’s running estimates with and without control variates.

Things to try:

  1. Defaults (posterior mean of , ). The degree-2 line sits on the dashed reference almost from the first checkpoint, while the plain average wanders. Over eight sets of 20 chains of length 5,000, degree 1 cuts the mean squared error by a factor of 11.6 to 29.9 and degree 2 by 183 to 473. New chain draws another set.
  2. Second moment. Choose . Degree 1 helps less, by 2.0 to 5.5 times, because the Poisson solution for a second moment is at least quadratic. Degree 2 gives 35.6 to 96.8.
  3. Tail probability. Choose . The reductions fall to 1.5 to 3.9 for degree 1 and 2.7 to 9.5 for degree 2. The gradient of an indicator’s Poisson solution has a kink at the threshold that no low-degree polynomial follows, and by Proposition 6 the gradient error is what remains.
  4. Chain length. At the degree-2 factor for the mean is 169 to 641 across the eight sets; at it is 148 to 676. The factor does not grow with , because the residual does not depend on it.

5 Constraints

  • First order only. Equation 5 is accurate when is small. On the two-mode target, where reaches 4.2, the exact bias is 1.33 times the prediction at .
  • Expectations under . The bias coefficient and the variance are expectations under the target, which is what the sampler is for. They explain the size, sign and scaling of the errors; computing them exactly needs the one-dimensional grid of the chart.
  • One dimension in the theorem. Theorem 4 is derived in one dimension. The -dimensional form is quoted, not derived. The chart’s exact computation also needs a grid, which only works in low dimension.
  • Dimension. For , ULA’s bias is per coordinate in whatever is, but in . A statistic summed over coordinates, or the joint law, needs a step that shrinks with .
  • Polynomial control variates. They help much less for non-smooth (item 3). Degree 2 needs coefficients fitted from the chain; South et al. (2023) regularise that fit for high dimensions. Fitting the coefficients on the same chain adds a small bias.
  • Minibatch gradients. Stochastic-gradient Langevin dynamics adds gradient noise to ULA’s discretisation error. With a fixed step its kernel has a stationary law and Proposition 3 applies to it. Teh, Thiery & Vollmer (2016) analyse decreasing steps, which have no stationary law, with Poisson-equation arguments of the same kind.
  • The grid. The chart is exact up to its 241-point grid and its truncation of the line to or . A 481-point grid moves no nonzero bias by more than 0.04%.

6 Next in the series

  • Part 6: Part 2’s normal approximation bounds how far a random neural network is from its Gaussian-process limit, and Part 1’s Gaussian integration by parts explains which directions one gradient step can find.
  • Part 7: the kernel Stein discrepancy as a training regulariser for VAE latents and JEPA embeddings.

Chains. Are. Operators. Their. Mismatch. Is. Bias. Their. Solution. Is. Variance.

7 References

  • Assaraf, R. & Caffarel, M. (1999). Zero-variance principle for Monte Carlo algorithms. Physical Review Letters 83(23), 4682–4685.
  • Dellaportas, P. & Kontoyiannis, I. (2012). Control variates for estimation based on reversible Markov chain Monte Carlo samplers. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B 74(1), 133–161.
  • Durmus, A. & Moulines, É. (2017). Nonasymptotic convergence analysis for the unadjusted Langevin algorithm. Annals of Applied Probability 27(3), 1551–1587.
  • Leimkuhler, B., Matthews, C. & Stoltz, G. (2016). The computation of averages from equilibrium and nonequilibrium Langevin molecular dynamics. IMA Journal of Numerical Analysis 36(1), 13–79.
  • Mattingly, J. C., Stuart, A. M. & Tretyakov, M. V. (2010). Convergence of numerical time-averaging and stationary measures via Poisson equations. SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis 48(2), 552–577.
  • Mira, A., Solgi, R. & Imparato, D. (2013). Zero variance Markov chain Monte Carlo for Bayesian estimators. Statistics and Computing 23(5), 653–662.
  • Roberts, G. O. & Tweedie, R. L. (1996). Exponential convergence of Langevin distributions and their discrete approximations. Bernoulli 2(4), 341–363.
  • South, L. F., Oates, C. J., Mira, A. & Drovandi, C. (2023). Regularized zero-variance control variates. Bayesian Analysis 18(3), 865–888.
  • Talay, D. & Tubaro, L. (1990). Expansion of the global error for numerical schemes solving stochastic differential equations. Stochastic Analysis and Applications 8(4), 483–509.
  • Teh, Y. W., Thiery, A. H. & Vollmer, S. J. (2016). Consistency and fluctuations for stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics. Journal of Machine Learning Research 17(7), 1–33.
  • Stein’s Method, Part 1: Stein’s Lemma — the identity and the Langevin operator.
  • Stein’s Method, Part 2: Normal Approximation — the Stein equation, its solution, and the generator approach.
  • Stein’s Method, Part 3: Kernel Stein Discrepancy and SVGD — KSD on MCMC output, Stein thinning and Stein control variates.
  • Stein’s Method, Part 4: Models Without Normalising Constants — score matching and Stein-based training losses.
  • Stein’s Method, Part 6: Neural Networks and Machine Learning — wide random networks, hidden directions, and a map of the series in machine learning.
  • Stein’s Method, Part 7: Kernel Stein Discrepancy as a Regulariser — KSD as a training loss, what its kernel lets it see, and a VAE and a JEPA on CIFAR-10.

item.title: Stein’s Method, Part 4: Models Without Normalising Constants
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
Energy-based and other unnormalised models are hard to fit by maximum likelihood, because the likelihood gradient needs the normalising constant. The model’s score in does not, and Stein’s identity turns that score into training objectives that never compute the constant.

Energy-based models write a density as up to a constant. Diffusion models train a network to output directly. Anyone who has fitted the first kind by maximum likelihood has run a sampler inside the training loop, because the likelihood gradient contains an expectation under the model itself. The -score of the same model costs one backward pass: the normalising constant is a function of alone, so it vanishes when differentiating in . Stein’s identity is the bridge from that cheap quantity to an objective whose minimum is the right model.

Part 1 showed that the Langevin Stein operator does not see the normalising constant, and derived Stein’s unbiased risk estimate (SURE). Part 2 turned Stein identities into distances. Part 3 made the distance computable with kernels and used its steepest-descent direction, SVGD, as a sampler. This part fits models with the same tools. Part 5 applies them to MCMC samplers, Part 6 to neural networks, and Part 7 to regularising learned representations.

An AI agent (Claude) drafted the text and the interactive charts. Separate review passes checked each derivation numerically and each reference against its source.

Two ideas carry the post:

  1. Score matching is Stein’s identity under the data. The unknown data score in the Fisher divergence is removed by one integration by parts, and the Fisher divergence equals a Stein discrepancy with an -penalised critic.
  2. Stein identities are training signals. Each tool from the earlier parts becomes a loss or a gradient with no normalising constant in it: SURE trains denoisers without clean data, the Gaussian identity builds unbiased control variates for policy gradients, and SVGD’s direction trains a sampler network.

1 Notation

  • : the data distribution, with density and score ; a sample from it.
  • : the model, with . For an energy-based model, .
  • : the model’s score in .
  • : a gradient in the parameters; and without a subscript act on .
  • : the Langevin Stein operator (Parts 1 and 3).
  • : the Fisher divergence.
  • and : the SURE setting of Part 1.

2 The maximum-likelihood gradient

Differentiate the log-likelihood of one point in :

The right-hand identity differentiates under the integral, then writes and . The maximum-likelihood gradient is therefore a difference of two expectations: one under the data, and one under the model. The second needs samples from at every step, usually from an MCMC chain run inside the training loop. The derivative in has no such term:

Smallest instance: with , so . Then , which needs the model’s second moment, while the score contains no trace of .

The density in the next chart is synthetic: , a two-component mixture written without its factors. The sample is 60 seeded draws from its normalised version. It stands in for an energy-based model whose constant is never computed.

The chart shows the same split for that fixed sample. Multiplying by a constant changes its total mass and the sample’s log-likelihood. It changes nothing computed from the score.

3 Score matching

The Fisher divergence compares scores directly:

It contains no , but it contains the data score , which is unknown. Integration by parts removes it.

Theorem 1 — score matching (Hyvärinen 2005, Theorem 1)

Proof.

4 Fisher divergence and the penalised Stein discrepancy

Part 2 defined the Stein discrepancy as over a class of critics , and Part 3 took the class to be a kernel ball. For a class closed under the absolute value can be dropped, as here. Taking every square-integrable critic, with a penalty on its size, recovers the Fisher divergence.

Proposition 2 — the L² Stein discrepancy

Let , and let be the set of fields with that satisfy Stein’s identity under , . If , then

Proof.

  1. Subtract the zero . The divergence terms cancel: .
  2. Maximise pointwise. For each , is a concave quadratic in , maximised at with value .
  3. Take expectations under .

Grathwohl et al. (2020) state this optimal critic. The value follows by substitution. In Hyvärinen’s normalisation it is . Score matching and the -penalised Stein discrepancy therefore have the same minimiser in .

4.1 Learning the critic

Grathwohl et al. (2020) train an energy-based model against a neural critic instead of computing the Laplacian:

  • Critic step. Ascend in . By Proposition 2, the maximum over all square-integrable critics is . A neural critic reaches it only as far as its family can represent , so the inner maximum approximates it from below.
  • Model step. Only the first term depends on , so . For , this is : one backward pass through the energy’s input gradient, with no samples from the model and no .

4.2 Minimum Stein discrepancy estimators

Barp et al. (2019) take this one step further. Any Stein operator and Stein set define an estimator

with the Stein discrepancy of Part 2 and the empirical distribution of the data. They show that score matching, contrastive divergence and minimum probability flow are special cases, each with its own operator and set, and they introduce diffusion versions of KSD and of score matching. Choosing the set decides the estimator:

Stein set Discrepancy Estimator
unit ball of KSD (Part 3) minimum KSD
unit ball of , supremum squared score matching (Barp et al. 2019, Theorem 2)
with penalty (Proposition 2) score matching
neural critics with penalty learned approximation of Grathwohl et al. (2020)

Over the unit ball of the supremum is , by Cauchy–Schwarz. The last two rows replace the ball by a penalty. The two exact rows are and , so they have the same minimiser in as score matching. The neural-critic row shares it only when the critic family can represent . Otherwise its inner maximum falls short of by an amount that can depend on , and so can its minimiser.

5 SURE as a training loss

Part 1 derived SURE from Gaussian integration by parts: for and a weakly differentiable estimator satisfying Part 1’s integrability conditions, the risk has an unbiased estimate that does not involve . Writing it in terms of instead of the correction :

Part 1’s form follows by substituting and .

5.1 Training a denoiser without clean data

Soltanayev & Chun (2018) train a denoising network on noisy images , , each with pixels, and known, and no clean . Equation 5 makes the expected loss computable from alone. The divergence of a network is expensive, so they estimate it by a random finite difference (Ramani, Blu & Unser 2008):

One draw of per image gives their training loss:

Its gradient follows from the chain rule, with :

That is two forward passes per image, and a backward pass through each.

  • What the first term does. On its own it would train to reproduce the noisy input, the identity map.
  • What the divergence term does. It penalises sensitivity to the input in proportion to , which is what keeps from copying the noise.
  • Settings in the paper. is redrawn every epoch. is small and fixed: for their MNIST denoiser and for DnCNN.

5.2 Choosing a regularisation strength

The same identity chooses a single parameter in closed form. For soft thresholding, , the correction is when and otherwise.

  1. .

This is the SURE criterion of Donoho & Johnstone (1995), stated there for . Their SureShrink applies it to each wavelet level, and falls back to the threshold on levels that look sparse. Minimising it over uses only . For ridge shrinkage, , the same steps give .

The signal in the chart is synthetic: 256 coordinates, 25 of them nonzero with magnitudes drawn between 2 and 6, observed once in Gaussian noise of known . It stands in for the wavelet coefficients of an image: a few large values among many near-zero ones. A wrong either keeps the noise (too small) or erases the signal (too large).

Things to try:

  1. At the defaults (soft threshold, ), SURE picks with a true loss of , while the oracle’s gives . The raw observation’s loss is .
  2. Press New noise draw several times. SURE’s curve is noisier than the loss curve, and its minimiser moves more. Over eight draws at , SURE’s ranges over and the oracle’s over . The loss at SURE’s is 0.3% to 22% above the oracle’s.
  3. Switch to ridge shrinkage. Over eight draws at , SURE’s stays within 0.10 of the oracle’s (up to 0.58 for soft thresholding), and the loss there is at most 0.6% above the oracle’s. On the first draw (reload the page to return to it), the best ridge loss is , against for soft thresholding. Shrinking every coordinate by the same factor cannot keep large values while zeroing small ones.
