On the first draw, SURE’s choice costs at most 2.3% more loss than the oracle’s up to , even where the two values differ by about 0.3, because the loss curve is flat near its minimum. At it costs 9% more. Over eight draws at each on the slider, the loss at SURE’s is at most 26% above the oracle’s (the worst case is at ). Equation 7 is unbiased for the risk at every , and summing over 256 coordinates keeps its noise small next to the risk.

6 Stein control variates for policy gradients

The policy-gradient theorem writes the gradient of expected return as . That is a score-function estimator, with high variance. Subtracting a baseline keeps it unbiased because . A baseline that also depends on the action, , can track much more closely, but it biases the gradient unless the term it adds is corrected for. Liu et al. (2018) supply the correction from Stein’s identity. In this section is a state, not a score, and is the map that turns noise into an action (Liu et al. write ).

Proposition 3 — Stein’s identity for reparameterisable policies (Liu et al. 2018, Theorem 3.1)

Let the action be with independent of , and let be differentiable. Under conditions that allow differentiation under the integral,

Proof. Compute two ways.

  1. Score function. , the left side of Equation 8.
  2. Reparameterisation. , the right side.

Both compute the same derivative.

For a Gaussian policy with mean and fixed covariance , , and Equation 8 with respect to the mean parameters reduces to . That is Part 1’s Gaussian integration by parts in the action.

Adding and subtracting gives the Stein control-variate gradient, unbiased for every (Liu et al. 2018, eq. 8):

  • The estimator. The sample version averages the bracket over observed , with an estimate in place of .
  • Fitting . Liu et al. parametrise . They fit either by regressing on observed returns, or by minimising the squared norm of the bracket in Equation 9, a direct proxy for the estimator’s variance. That objective mixes derivatives in and , which the paper finds hard to compute efficiently with automatic differentiation. For Gaussian policies it minimises instead, the variances of the gradient estimates for the policy’s mean and covariance.
  • Keeping it unbiased. Fitting on the same data the gradient uses biases the estimate. Liu et al. note that fitting on the previous iteration’s data removes the bias. Their experiments use the current data, and a check with previous-iteration data did not improve results.
  • Smallest instance. , with no action dependence, gives , and Equation 9 reduces to the ordinary baseline.

7 Amortised SVGD

SVGD (Part 3) moves a fixed set of particles. A sampler network , , needs a rule for moving its weights instead. Wang & Liu (2016) pull SVGD’s direction back through the network.

  1. Draw and set .

  2. Compute the SVGD direction on this batch, .

  3. Ask the network to output instead. One gradient step on at the current , with unit step length, gives their update:

The gradient of that squared error at the current is , so the step is backpropagation of SVGD’s direction through the generator.

  • Smallest instance. A location family, , has . The repulsion terms cancel in the sum over , because for a translation-invariant kernel. The update reduces to , which moves the network’s location toward high target density.
  • A direct KSD penalty. The alternative minimises itself (Part 3). Its gradient in is , and contains , so it needs , the Hessian of . Amortised SVGD needs only . Both are free of .
  • In this blog. Nuisance Leakage in JEPA Embeddings uses a KSD penalty toward on an encoder’s embeddings. That target has , which makes the Hessian term free.

8 Constraints

  • Kernel and bandwidth. KSD-based objectives inherit Part 3’s kernel choice: light-tailed kernels can certify a non-converging sample in , and a bad bandwidth stalls or over-smooths SVGD.
  • Dimension. Kernel distances between points concentrate as grows, which should be expected to weaken KSD tests and SVGD’s repulsion. Anastasiou et al. (2023) list sliced Stein discrepancies as one way to cut the cost of Stein discrepancies in high dimensions.
  • Low-density regions. weights score errors by . Where the data are rare, a wrong score costs almost nothing, so a fitted score is least reliable where a sampler started from noise begins.
  • Isolated components. Fisher divergence, KSD and SVGD cannot see the mixing weights of well-separated components (Wenliang & Kanagawa 2020). Part 3’s chart reproduces this: a sample sitting entirely on the lighter mode has a lower KSD than an exact sample.
  • Second derivatives. Score matching needs , which is backward passes. A learned critic replaces it with , which avoids differentiating the energy twice but is still passes when computed exactly. A random-projection estimate, as in Equation 6, cuts either trace to one pass per probe at the cost of variance.
  • SURE’s assumptions. SURE needs Gaussian noise with known and a weakly differentiable estimator. With a Monte Carlo divergence, trades the finite-difference bias against round-off.

9 Next in the series

  • Part 5: the Langevin operator applied to gradients is the generator of the Langevin diffusion. Its Stein equation is the Poisson equation of MCMC, whose solution sets the bias of unadjusted Langevin and the variance of exact samplers.
  • Part 6: Stein’s lemma bounds how far a random network is from a Gaussian process and explains which directions one gradient step can learn; its closing map places score matching, SURE and SVGD in machine learning.
  • Part 7: the kernel Stein discrepancy of a batch of codes as a regulariser in a VAE and a JEPA, compared with KL, MMD, VICReg and SIGReg.

10 Further reading

  • Anastasiou et al. (2023) review Stein’s method in computational statistics: discrepancies, samplers, goodness-of-fit tests and estimators.
  • Ley, Reinert & Swan (2017) survey Stein operators for univariate distributions, beyond the Langevin form used in this series.
  • Barp et al. (2019) give the general minimum Stein discrepancy framework, with consistency, asymptotic normality and robustness results.
  • Part 1, Part 2 and Part 3 of this series derive every identity Part 4 uses.

Constants. Cancel. Scores. Remain. Stein. Turns. Scores. Into. Losses.

item.title: Stein’s Method, Part 3: Kernel Stein Discrepancy and SVGD
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
The kernel Stein discrepancy (KSD) measures how far a sample is from a target density using only the target’s score, in closed form. Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) moves a set of particles along the direction in which the same kernel says KL divergence falls fastest.

MCMC output is usually checked with trace plots, and effective sample size. Those compare chains with one another, not with the target. A sampler with a bias, such as unadjusted Langevin with a large step or stochastic-gradient Langevin with minibatch noise, can mix well and settle on the wrong distribution, and every between-chain check still passes. Catching that needs a comparison of the sample with the target itself. The target is usually known only up to its normalising constant, so the comparison has to go through the score. Part 2’s Stein discrepancy does this, but it is a supremum over a class of functions. Taking that class to be a ball in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space turns the supremum into a double sum.

Part 1 built the Langevin Stein operator and showed that it does not see the normalising constant. Part 2 turned Stein identities into distances. Part 4 uses the same discrepancy to fit models. Part 5 predicts the bias and variance of MCMC samplers instead of measuring them after the run. Part 6 turns to neural networks, and Part 7 adds this part’s discrepancy to training losses.

An AI agent (Claude) drafted the text and the interactive chart. Separate review passes checked each derivation numerically and each reference against its source.

Three ideas carry the post:

  1. Kernel Stein discrepancy. With ranging over the unit ball of a kernel’s Hilbert space, has a closed form: the square root of for an explicit Stein kernel .
  2. SVGD. The function that attains that supremum is the direction of steepest descent of among small kernel-smooth moves of the sample. Moving particles along it is a sampler.
  3. Stein control variates. has mean zero under for every in the Stein class, so it can be subtracted from an integrand to reduce Monte Carlo variance.

1 Notation

  • : the target density on ; an unnormalised version; its score.
  • : the law of the sample; the sample.
  • for a vector field (Part 1).
  • : a positive definite kernel; its reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), in which .
  • : vector fields with each , and .
  • Two kernels:
    • RBF, , with bandwidth .
    • Inverse multiquadric (IMQ), with and . The default is , .

2 Stein’s identity in dimensions

Part 1 proved the one-dimensional identity and stated this one. The KSD closed form, the SVGD direction and the control variates all rest on it.

Proposition 1 — the Langevin identity in

Let be positive and continuously differentiable on , and let be a continuously differentiable vector field with and . Then

Proof.

  1. , by the product rule.
  2. On the ball of radius , the divergence theorem gives , where is the outward normal.
  3. Write . In polar coordinates, , so cannot stay bounded away from zero. There is a sequence with , and the boundary flux in step 2 is at most in absolute value.
  4. Along , the left side of step 2 tends to by dominated convergence, and the right side tends to 0.

The integrability of under plays the role of Part 1’s condition that vanishes at an infinite end.

3 Kernel Stein discrepancy

Part 2 defined the Stein discrepancy and left the supremum as an optimisation. A Hilbert-space ball makes it a projection. The closed form uses two RKHS facts:

  • Reproducing property. .
  • Derivative reproducing property. If has continuous mixed partial derivatives , then . Here is the derivative in the first argument, and it is itself in .
Definition — kernel Stein discrepancy

The ball is symmetric, so the supremum of the expectation equals the supremum of its absolute value.

Theorem 2 — closed form (Liu, Lee & Jordan 2016; Chwialkowski, Strathmann & Gretton 2016)

Let have continuous mixed partial derivatives, and define the Stein kernel

If , then

with and independent.

The formula is from the two papers in the title. The integrability condition is the one in Gorham & Mackey (2017, Proposition 2); Chwialkowski et al. assume the stronger .

Proof.

  1. The operator as an inner product. For , the two reproducing properties give

  2. Take expectations inside. Expanding with the reproducing properties gives the -th term of . So . Each is therefore Bochner integrable (integrable as a random element of ), lies in , and .

  3. The supremum is a norm. with . By Cauchy–Schwarz its supremum over the unit ball is , attained at .

  4. Expand the norm. . Expanding each inner product with the reproducing properties gives the four terms of Equation 2, coordinate by coordinate.

Three consequences:

  • No normalising constant. depends on only through , which is the same for and (Part 1).
  • No samples from . Only the sample from enters.
  • Zero at the target. For fixed , is applied to the field . When and its first and mixed second derivatives are bounded, as for the RBF and IMQ kernels, and , that field meets the conditions of Proposition 1. Then Equation 1 gives , and .

Smallest instance. Take , (so ) and the RBF kernel. With , , and . The four terms collapse to

3.1 Estimators

Replacing by the sample gives two estimators of , each to compute:

  • V-statistic, . It is the squared KSD of the empirical measure itself, so it is never negative. It is biased upward: its mean is .
  • U-statistic, . It is unbiased for and can be negative.

Goodness-of-fit tests use these as test statistics. When the U-statistic is degenerate, so its limit law is not normal, and the tests calibrate with a bootstrap. Liu, Lee & Jordan (2016) use the U-statistic. Chwialkowski, Strathmann & Gretton (2016) use the V-statistic with a wild bootstrap, which reweights the terms with random signs drawn along the chain and so also handles correlated MCMC samples.

The V-statistic does not vanish on an exact sample at finite . For 100 exact draws from the banana target of Section 5, the IMQ KSD ranges from 0.30 to 0.43 over five seeds. That is the noise floor any finite i.i.d. sample sits on.

3.2 Kernel choice

Gorham & Mackey (2017) separate kernels that make KSD a reliable convergence check from kernels that do not:

  • Light tails fail in . For the standard normal target in , KSD with the Gaussian, Matérn or compactly supported Wendland kernel can go to zero along a sequence of samples that does not converge to the target (their Theorem 6). The kernel’s features decay too fast to penalise mass drifting away.
  • IMQ succeeds. With the IMQ kernel (, ), implies weak convergence for every target that is distantly dissipative with a Lipschitz score (their Theorem 8). Distantly dissipative means the score points back toward the bulk at long range, with . Their examples include finite Gaussian mixtures with a common covariance, and Bayesian linear, logistic and Huber regression posteriors with Gaussian priors. Of the chart’s three targets only the mixture is in this class: the banana’s score grows like and is not distantly dissipative along the ridge, and the donut’s score is not Lipschitz at the origin.
  • One dimension is safe. In , for targets in the same distantly dissipative class, any kernel with twice continuously differentiable and a non-vanishing generalised Fourier transform works, Gaussian included (their Theorem 5). Neither Theorem 5 nor Theorem 6 covers , so for Gaussian and Matérn kernels in two dimensions the paper says nothing either way.

The chart in Section 5 uses the IMQ kernel with and , the default of Gorham & Mackey (2017). Its targets are two-dimensional, so it cannot show the failure.

4 Stein variational gradient descent

KSD measures a distance, and its maximiser is a direction: the direction in which the sample most violates Stein’s identity. Moving the sample along that direction reduces the KL divergence fastest.

Theorem 3 — steepest descent of KL (Liu & Wang 2016, Theorem 3.1 and Lemma 3.2)

Let and be smooth positive densities. For a smooth field and small , let , and let be the law of when . Under regularity conditions that allow differentiation under the integral,

Over with , the fastest decrease is , attained at , where

Proof.

  1. Move the map onto . KL divergence is unchanged when the same invertible map is applied to both arguments. So , and has density .
  2. Write it out. . For small the determinant is positive.
  3. Differentiate at . and . Together these give Equation 4.
  4. Optimise over the ball. By step 3 of Theorem 2’s proof, , which is maximised over the unit ball at with value . By the reproducing property, , which is Equation 5.

Liu & Wang (2016) state the same result over the ball of radius , where the optimal direction is itself and the derivative is .

4.1 The particle update

Replace by the current particles and step along (Liu & Wang 2016, Algorithm 1):

  • Driving force. A kernel-weighted average of the scores at nearby particles pulls toward high density, smoothed over the bandwidth.
  • Repulsion. For the RBF kernel, . It points from toward , so it pushes particles apart. Without it, every particle would climb to a mode.
  • One particle. With , for a translation-invariant kernel, and Equation 6 becomes gradient ascent on . One SVGD particle finds a mode.
  • Bandwidth. Liu & Wang (2016) write the RBF kernel as and set , where is the median pairwise distance between particles, so that . In this post’s convention, that is .
  • Step size. Liu & Wang use AdaGrad, which scales each coordinate’s step by its past gradients. The chart uses a fixed , so that the comparison with Langevin uses one step size for both.

4.2 Gradient flow

As and then , with time measured as times the number of steps, the limiting particle density follows the continuity equation (Liu 2017). Along it the KL divergence falls at a rate set by the KSD (Liu 2017, Theorem 3.4):

  • The second equality integrates by parts once, with boundary terms assumed to vanish.
  • The third applies Equation 1 under : .
  • The fourth is step 4 of Theorem 3, with .

Langevin dynamics obeys the same identity with the Fisher divergence in place of (Liu 2017, §3.5). Part 4 returns to that divergence.

5 SVGD and Langevin on three targets

The targets are synthetic two-dimensional densities, each written as an unnormalised log-density and its score. Each stands in for a posterior shape that breaks simpler samplers:

  • Banana: and . A curved ridge, like the posterior of a model that identifies only a product or a square of its parameters.
  • Mixture: with separation . Two explanations of the data with unequal weight.
  • Donut: . Mass on a ring, like a posterior constrained near a sphere.

A wrong answer here means reporting posterior means and intervals from a sample that misses part of the target, or weights it wrongly.

The comparison holds the budget fixed. SVGD moves particles; unadjusted Langevin (ULA) runs independent chains, with . Both start from the same points and use the same step size and number of iterations, so both make score evaluations per iteration. SVGD also pays kernel evaluations per iteration, which the count leaves out.

The chart shows both point sets over the target’s contours, and their KSD against score evaluations.

Things to try:

  1. Defaults (banana, , , median-heuristic bandwidth). Press Play. Langevin is ahead at first: after 50 iterations its KSD is lower on all five seeds checked (0.27 to 0.40, against 0.42 to 0.61 for SVGD). Langevin’s trace is noisy, so the two curves cross back and forth for a while: SVGD first drops below it between iterations 31 and 61, and stays below from somewhere between iteration 77 and 119, depending on the seed. After 500 iterations it reaches 0.060 to 0.067, against 0.22 to 0.38 for Langevin, which sits near the 0.30 to 0.43 floor of 100 exact draws.
  2. Step size. Press Reset, set to 0.1 and press Play. Langevin diverges on the banana on every seed checked, because its step is too large for the score’s steep walls. From this start SVGD stays finite up to 0.2 on all 20 seeds checked, because the kernel average damps each particle’s step. Its stability has limits. Started at with , SVGD diverges on 5 of 10 seeds, and the widget then marks it as diverged too.
  3. Bandwidth. Press Reset, untick the median heuristic, set and press Play. The kernel weight between distinct particles is now close to zero, so the driving force shrinks to about : each particle runs its own gradient ascent with step , and only near neighbours still repel. The particles slide onto the ridge and bunch closer to it than the target does, and KSD is still 0.72 to 0.97 after 500 iterations. Press Reset again and set : the kernel averages scores over too wide an area, and KSD ends at 0.16 to 0.24. With (after another Reset) it ends at 0.051 to 0.067, about where the median heuristic lands (0.055 to 0.070, with settling near 0.57). These ranges cover 20 seeds, so they hold however many times Reset has been pressed.
  4. Missing mode. Choose the mixture, set the separation to 8 and the initial centre to 4, so every particle starts on the lighter mode. After 1,000 iterations SVGD has kept all of them there: the share with is 1.00, against a target of 0.30. Across 20 seeds KSD reads 0.042 to 0.051, lower than for 100 exact draws from the mixture (0.16 to 0.25). The heavy mode is too far away for the kernel or the score to see.
  5. Same mixture, centred start. Set . The particles split between the modes, but after 1,000 iterations 0.33 to 0.54 of them sit on the lighter one across 20 seeds, with a median of 0.43. Exact draws would put 0.30 there, give or take 0.05.

Item 4 is a blindness of score-based methods in general: far from a component, the score carries almost no information about that component’s weight (Wenliang & Kanagawa 2020). A low KSD certifies the sample against the score, and the score does not know about modes it has not visited.

6 Using KSD on MCMC output

The same discrepancy that drives SVGD can audit any sampler’s output.

6.1 A sample-quality check

Compute the KSD of a sampler’s output against . Unlike between-chain diagnostics, it compares the sample with the target. It can therefore rank step sizes or approximate samplers by how close their output is to , not only by how well they mix. Gorham & Mackey (2015) introduced Stein discrepancies for this purpose. Liu, Lee & Jordan (2016) and Chwialkowski et al. (2016) gave the kernel closed form, and Gorham & Mackey (2017) showed which kernels make it a reliable convergence check.

6.2 Stein thinning

MCMC output is usually thinned by keeping every tenth or hundredth point after a burn-in. Stein thinning (Riabiz et al. 2022) instead picks points greedily to make the selected set’s KSD small:

The rule is greedy minimisation of the V-statistic. Adding a point to a selected set of size raises the double sum , which is of the enlarged set, by , half of which is Equation 7.

  • Points are selected with replacement, so an index can repeat.
  • The cost is at most for selected points.
  • Riabiz et al. use an IMQ base kernel with a preconditioner.

6.3 Stein points

Stein points (Chen et al. 2018) use the same greedy objective, minimised over all of instead of over a chain’s output, starting from a global maximum of . That start agrees with the objective: at the first step it is alone, and for the IMQ kernel , which every stationary point of minimises.

7 Stein control variates

Estimating by a sample average has variance . Subtracting a function with known mean zero leaves the mean unchanged and can cut the variance. Stein’s identity produces such functions from any in the Stein class, using only the score.

Proposition 4 — Stein control variates

Let satisfy the conditions of Proposition 1, and let . Assume and have finite variance under , and that is positive definite. Then, for every :

  1. .
  2. is minimised at , where .
  3. The minimum is , where is the squared multiple correlation between and .

Proof.

  1. by Equation 1.
  2. , a convex quadratic in . Its gradient vanishes at .
  3. Substituting, .

Smallest instance. Take and , which has .

  • gives .
  • gives .
  • With alone, and , so the variance falls from 3 to 2 ().
  • With both, : zero variance, and the estimate is exact.

Polynomial remove polynomial completely under a Gaussian target.

In practice is estimated from the same sample, which adds a small bias unless the sample is split.

Control functionals (Oates, Girolami & Chopin 2017) let range over instead of a finite family. Then ranges over an RKHS whose kernel is the Stein kernel of Equation 2. Adding constants gives the kernel .

  1. Fit. Fit by kernel ridge regression with . The fit is with , where and .

  2. Integrate the fit. (Section 3), so , and the fitted function integrates to .

  3. Simplify. With and the Sherman–Morrison formula,

This is a weighted sum of the , with weights that do not depend on and sum to just under one for small . Oates et al. define the estimator with sample splitting, where one part of the sample fits and the other averages, and prove a mean squared error of under their conditions. They recommend the unsplit form Equation 8 for its lower variance.

8 Unnormalised posteriors

For a Bayesian posterior , with prior and likelihood , the score is

The evidence never appears. KSD (Equation 2), the SVGD direction (Equation 5), Stein thinning (Equation 7) and control functionals (Equation 8) take only from the target.

Smallest instance: logistic regression with a prior, features and labels . The score is , with the logistic function. It costs one pass over the data, the same as a gradient step.

9 Constraints

  • Mode blindness. KSD and SVGD see only the score along the sample. A component far from every particle contributes nothing, so a sample that misses it can have a lower KSD than an exact sample (item 4).
  • Kernel choice. In , light-tailed kernels can certify a non-converging sample. Use IMQ with for convergence checks.
  • Dimension. Each kernel evaluation compares -dimensional vectors, and kernel distances concentrate as grows, so KSD tests and SVGD’s repulsion should be expected to weaken in high dimensions. Neither is checked here beyond .
  • Cost. KSD, SVGD and Stein thinning are per evaluation or step. Control functionals solve an linear system.
  • Bandwidth. Too small a bandwidth turns SVGD into slow independent gradient ascent, and too large a bandwidth over-smooths it (item 3). The median heuristic is a rule of thumb, not a guarantee.
  • Finite-sample floor. The V-statistic KSD of an exact i.i.d. sample is positive: 0.30 to 0.43 for 100 banana draws. Interacting particles can go below it, and so can a sample that misses a mode (item 4), so a value below the floor does not by itself certify a sample.

10 Next in the series

  • Part 4 turns the same machinery on model fitting. With a ball in instead of an RKHS, the Stein discrepancy becomes the square root of the Fisher divergence of score matching; with an penalty in place of the ball, it becomes the Fisher divergence itself, up to a constant. Stein identities then supply training losses for denoisers, control variates for policy gradients, and a generator update that pulls SVGD’s direction back to network weights.
  • Part 5 returns to MCMC. The Langevin operator applied to gradients is the generator of the Langevin diffusion; its Stein equation gives unadjusted Langevin’s bias to first order in the step, the asymptotic variance of exact samplers, and Section 7’s control variates restricted to gradient fields.
  • Part 6 applies Stein’s lemma to neural networks and maps where KSD and SVGD are used in machine learning.
  • Part 7 uses KSD to N(0, I) as a training regulariser: the length of the SVGD step a batch of codes would take. In 64 dimensions a wide kernel sees little more than the first two moments.
  • Nuisance Leakage in JEPA Embeddings uses KSD to with an IMQ kernel as an anti-collapse regulariser for a self-supervised encoder.

Kernels. Close. The. Supremum. Particles. Follow. It. Modes. Hide.

item.title: Stein’s Method, Part 2: Normal Approximation
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
Stein’s method bounds the distance between a random variable’s law and the normal by solving one differential equation per test function. For a normalised sum of independent terms it gives a Wasserstein distance of order , with explicit constants.

Normal approximations are usually justified by the central limit theorem and a rule of thumb such as . The theorem is a limit statement: it says the error goes to zero, not how large it is at the in hand. Thirty summands are plenty for a uniform, whose standardised sum is then from the normal in Wasserstein distance. They are nowhere near enough for a Bernoulli with , where the distance at is . Berry–Esseen-type theorems give a rate. Stein’s method proves one in a page, with constants that can be computed, and the same template extends to dependent terms and to other limit laws.

Part 1 showed that over a rich class of characterises the standard normal, and that its proof writes as an expectation of that form. This part makes that equality quantitative. Part 3 makes the resulting discrepancy computable from samples, Part 4 uses it to fit models, Part 5 runs the generator approach on MCMC samplers, Part 6 applies Theorem 4 and its refinements to random neural networks, and Part 7 trains with the discrepancy as a regulariser.

An AI agent (Claude) drafted the text and the interactive chart. Separate review passes checked each derivation numerically and each reference against its source.

Three ideas carry the post:

  1. The Stein equation. For a test function , the solution of converts the error into , an expectation under alone.
  2. Bounds on the solution. For Lipschitz , and its first two derivatives are bounded by constant multiples of . A bound on that holds uniformly over that small class of therefore bounds the Wasserstein distance.

5 Sums of independent terms

Lemma 3 places every with in the class

5.1 The bound against exact distances

The summands are synthetic. Four laws, each standardised to mean 0 and variance 1, cover the cases the theorem treats differently. Each stands in for a quantity averaged over independent units:

  • Exponential: a waiting time, continuous and skewed.
  • Uniform: a rounding error, continuous and symmetric.
  • Skewed mixture: a cost with a minority of large values. Each draw comes from with probability 0.85 and from with probability 0.15.

  • the incomplete gamma function for the exponential;
  • the Irwin–Hall distribution function (the law of a sum of uniforms), on a fine grid, for the uniform;

6 Other couplings and operators

Leave-one-out needs independence. The same Stein equation and the same bounds on support other ways of controlling . All four need posts of their own, so here they get one line each.

  • Exchangeable pairs (Stein 1986): build with exchangeable and , then expand . This handles statistics of a whole dependent system, such as the anti-voter model (Ross 2011, §3.3.1); local dependence is usually handled with dependency neighbourhoods instead (Ross 2011, §3.2).
  • Zero-bias couplings (Goldstein & Reinert 1997; Goldstein 2010): build with . Then , which is at most . By Part 1, the normal is the only law with .
  • Chen–Stein Poisson approximation (Chen 1975): the Poisson() law has its own operator, , and the same template bounds the distance from a count of rare, weakly dependent events to the Poisson.
  • The generator approach (Barbour 1988, 1990): choose a Markov process whose stationary law is the target. Its generator is a Stein operator. For the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, Section 4 shows its semigroup solving the Stein equation.

7 The Stein discrepancy

Replace by a density on and the Gaussian operator by the Langevin operator of Part 1. Replace by a sample from a law . The supremum in Corollary 2 becomes the Stein discrepancy (Gorham & Mackey 2015), with called the Stein set:

  • What it needs. Samples from , to estimate , and the score . It does not need ’s normalising constant, since (Part 1). It does not need samples from .
  • Why it measures distance. If contains a solution of for every , the argument of Corollary 2 gives . Bounding those solutions for a non-Gaussian plays the role of Lemma 3, and is harder.
  • Why it is hard to compute. The supremum is an optimisation over functions. Gorham & Mackey (2015) solve it as a linear program over a graph built on the sample points.

Smallest instance: in one dimension and . By Equation 3, exactly.

8 Constraints

  • Moments. Theorem 4 needs ; the zero-bias route needs third moments. Heavier tails fall outside both.
  • Independence. Step 1 of the proof uses , which fails under dependence. Exchangeable pairs and couplings (Section 6) are the replacements.
  • Wasserstein, not Kolmogorov. Converting through halves the rate to . A direct Kolmogorov bound needs the non-smooth .
  • Constants. The bound exceeds the exact distance by 3.6 to 15.5 times at for the Bernoulli, exponential and mixture laws in the chart, and by 443 times for the uniform, whose true rate is .

9 Next in the series

  • Part 3: with the unit ball of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space of vector fields, Equation 5 becomes a double expectation of a kernel. It is computed from samples in time, and its steepest-descent direction moves particles toward .
  • Part 4: with a ball in , the same discrepancy becomes the Fisher divergence that score matching minimises, up to a square or a constant.
  • Part 5: the generator approach of Section 6, run for the Langevin diffusion. Its Stein equation is the Poisson equation, whose solution gives the bias of unadjusted Langevin and the variance of MCMC averages.
  • Part 6: Theorem 4 applies to a random network’s output, a sum over hidden units. Conditioning on the hidden layer improves its to .
  • Part 7: the Stein discrepancy of a batch of codes as a training loss for a VAE and a JEPA.

Solve. Stein’s. Equation. Bound. Solutions. Leave. One. Out. Rates. Follow.

  • Gorham, J. & Mackey, L. (2015). Measuring sample quality with Stein’s method. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 28.

  • Stein’s Method, Part 3: Kernel Stein Discrepancy and SVGD — a closed-form Stein discrepancy and sampling by particles.
  • Stein’s Method, Part 4: Models Without Normalising Constants — score matching and Stein-based training losses.
  • Stein’s Method, Part 5: Markov Chain Monte Carlo — the Poisson equation, the bias of unadjusted Langevin and zero-variance control variates.
  • Stein’s Method, Part 6: Neural Networks and Machine Learning — wide random networks, hidden directions, and a map of the series in machine learning.
  • Stein’s Method, Part 7: Kernel Stein Discrepancy as a Regulariser — KSD as a training loss, what its kernel lets it see, and a VAE and a JEPA on CIFAR-10.

item.title: Stein’s Method, Part 1: Stein’s Lemma
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
Stein’s lemma characterises the standard normal by one expectation identity that must hold for every test function in a class, instead of by a list of moments. Rewritten for any smooth density, the identity needs only the derivative of the log-density, so it still works when the density’s normalising constant is unknown.

Checking whether data look normal usually means a histogram, a QQ plot, or the first few moments. Moments are a weak check. After standardising, the uniform, the Laplace and the normal share their mean and variance, and no finite list of matched moments pins a law down. Stein’s lemma replaces the list with one identity required of a whole class of test functions. Each contributes one equation, and the class as a whole leaves only the normal standing. The general-density version is what makes the idea useful beyond normality: it tests a sample against a density whose integral nobody can compute.

This is the first of seven parts. Part 2 turns the identity into a bound on the distance between a sum and the normal. Part 3 makes that distance computable from samples and uses it to move particles toward a target. Part 4 fits models whose normalising constant is unknown. Part 5 gives the bias and variance of MCMC samplers. Part 6 applies the identity to neural networks. Part 7 uses the discrepancy built from it as a training regulariser.

An AI agent (Claude) drafted the text and the interactive chart. Separate review passes checked each derivation numerically and each reference against its source.

Three ideas carry the post:

  1. Stein’s identity. holds for every suitable when , and for no other law.
  2. The Langevin Stein operator. The same construction for a density uses only through its score , so an unknown normalising constant drops out.
  3. Stein’s unbiased risk estimate (SURE). For a Gaussian observation, the identity turns an estimator’s expected squared error, which depends on the unknown mean, into a quantity computed from the data.

5 The Langevin Stein operator

Lemma 1’s proof used one property of : the ratio . Any positive, differentiable density has such a ratio, its score . The same integration by parts goes through with in place of . The product rule gives , which defines the operator:

5.1 Unnormalised densities

Suppose is known only up to a constant: can be evaluated at any , but cannot be computed. Bayesian posteriors are the standard case. The prior times the likelihood is known pointwise, and its integral, the evidence, is not. The score does not see the constant:

5.3 Testing the identity by simulation

The draws are synthetic: seeded pseudo-random samples from the four laws in the table. Standardising them removes location and scale, so any difference between them is shape. They stand in for a sample whose law is in question. A wrong conclusion would mean accepting a non-normal law as normal on the strength of a check that cannot tell them apart, such as matching the mean and variance.

6 Stein’s unbiased risk estimate

The Gaussian identity also has a use that tests no distribution. Suppose we estimate a normal mean from one noisy observation. The estimator’s error depends on the unknown mean, so it cannot be computed from the data. Stein (1981) used Equation 4 to remove that dependence.

  • Observation. , with known and unknown.
  • Estimator. for a correction ; is the maximum-likelihood estimate .
  • Risk. , a function of the unknown .
Proposition 5 — SURE (identity due to Stein 1981)

Let each coordinate be absolutely continuous along almost every line parallel to the -th axis, with , and finite. Then

The conditions are the ones the proof uses.

Proof.

  1. Expand: .
  2. .
  3. Apply Equation 4 to for each : . Summing over , .
  4. Take expectations in step 1 and substitute steps 2 and 3.

contains no , so it is computed from the observation alone. Its expectation equals the risk at every . Part 4 trains denoisers by minimising it and uses it to choose a regularisation strength.

6.1 James–Stein shrinkage

gives , the risk of . The James–Stein estimator (James & Stein 1961) shrinks toward the origin:

  1. .

  2. , so .

  3. Substituting into Equation 7:

  4. Conditions. is smooth except at , where and . All three integrability conditions hold when . For the second, Cauchy–Schwarz gives . That is the case for , where the singularity at 0 is integrable.

  5. Risk. for every . At , and , so . In , that is against .

For , the observation itself, the maximum-likelihood estimate, has strictly higher risk than at every . The proof is four lines of Equation 7.

7 Constraints

  • Boundary terms. The identity needs the boundary term to vanish. On the whole line, is enough. A density that stays positive at an end of a bounded support, as for the uniform or a truncated normal, breaks it unless takes the same value at both ends, for instance because vanishes there. The uniform with gives 3, not 0.
  • Integrability. binds for heavy tails. Under Student-, needs for the Langevin operator and for the Gaussian one, and Monte Carlo error bars need and respectively.
  • One test function is one equation. A characterisation needs a class rich enough to see the distribution function; Lemma 2’s class is one, because it contains the indicator solutions . With alone, every standardised law passes.
  • Densities only. The score needs absolutely continuous on its support. A law with atoms has no score; Stein operators for discrete laws use differences instead (Ley, Reinert & Swan 2017).
  • SURE’s assumptions. SURE needs Gaussian noise, a known , and a weakly differentiable estimator. Hard thresholding jumps, so its divergence has a point mass that Equation 7 leaves out.

8 Next in the series

  • Part 2: Lemma 2’s proof solved the Stein equation for one indicator. Solving it for every test function in a class turns a small into a bound on a distance between and , with explicit constants, and gives the central limit theorem with a rate.
  • Part 3: the -dimensional Langevin operator, with ranging over a kernel space, gives a discrepancy that is computed from a sample and the score, with no normalising constant.
  • Part 4: SURE returns as a training loss, and the score’s blindness to becomes the main tool for fitting unnormalised models.
  • Part 5: the Langevin operator applied to gradients is the generator of the Langevin diffusion, and its Stein equation gives the bias of unadjusted Langevin and the variance of exact samplers.
  • Part 6: Proposition 3 and Price’s theorem bound how far a random network is from a Gaussian process, give its limit kernels, and recover a hidden direction from input–output pairs.
  • Part 7: the identity, tested on a batch of codes over a class of functions, becomes a training loss. Over affine functions it is the moment penalty of self-supervised learning.

One. Identity. Pins. Normals. Scores. Ignore. Constants. Boundaries. Decide.

9 References

  • Gorham, J. & Mackey, L. (2015). Measuring sample quality with Stein’s method. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 28.
  • Gorham, J. & Mackey, L. (2017). Measuring sample quality with kernels. Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 70, 1292–1301.
  • James, W. & Stein, C. (1961). Estimation with quadratic loss. Proceedings of the Fourth Berkeley Symposium on Mathematical Statistics and Probability 1, 361–379.
  • Ley, C., Reinert, G. & Swan, Y. (2017). Stein’s method for comparison of univariate distributions. Probability Surveys 14, 1–52.
  • Price, R. (1958). A useful theorem for nonlinear devices having Gaussian inputs. IRE Transactions on Information Theory 4(2), 69–72.
  • Ross, N. (2011). Fundamentals of Stein’s method. Probability Surveys 8, 210–293.
  • Stein, C. (1972). A bound for the error in the normal approximation to the distribution of a sum of dependent random variables. Proceedings of the Sixth Berkeley Symposium on Mathematical Statistics and Probability 2, 583–602.
  • Stein, C. M. (1981). Estimation of the mean of a multivariate normal distribution. Annals of Statistics 9(6), 1135–1151.
  • Stein’s Method, Part 2: Normal Approximation — the Stein equation, bounds on its solution, and a Wasserstein bound for sums.
  • Stein’s Method, Part 3: Kernel Stein Discrepancy and SVGD — the -dimensional operator with kernels, and sampling by particles.
  • Stein’s Method, Part 4: Models Without Normalising Constants — score matching and Stein-based training losses.
  • Stein’s Method, Part 5: Markov Chain Monte Carlo — the Poisson equation, the bias of unadjusted Langevin and zero-variance control variates.
  • Stein’s Method, Part 6: Neural Networks and Machine Learning — wide random networks, hidden directions, and a map of the series in machine learning.
  • Stein’s Method, Part 7: Kernel Stein Discrepancy as a Regulariser — KSD as a training loss, what its kernel lets it see, and a VAE and a JEPA on CIFAR-10.

item.title: Nuisance Leakage in JEPA Embeddings Is Set by Regulariser Strength and Width
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
Self-supervised image encoders keep some detail they were meant to ignore; on rendered images where that detail is known, the amount is set mainly by how hard the anti-collapse regulariser pushes and by the embedding width, not by which target distribution it pushes toward.

Anyone who has trained a contrastive or predictive encoder has written an augmentation pipeline: crop, flip, recolour. The pipeline encodes a wish: whatever it changes, the encoder should ignore. The training loss never checks the wish. On photographs it cannot be checked, because nobody has a list of everything that differs between two views. A rendered dataset with known generating factors supplies that list and turns the wish into a number.

Three ideas carry the results:

  1. Leakage: how well a simple probe reads the ignored factors back out of the embedding. Known factors make it measurable.
  2. Regulariser strength, not the target law, controls leakage.
  3. Embedding width is a better nuisance filter than injected noise here.

An AI agent (Claude) ran the experiments unattended and drafted the text. Every number below comes from the study’s result files through its report script, and a separate review pass recomputed them from the raw runs.

1 Joint-embedding prediction

A joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA; Assran et al. 2023) learns from pairs of views of one scene.

  • An encoder maps an image to an embedding of numbers.
  • A small predictor maps view 1’s embedding to a guess at view 2’s embedding.
  • Training lowers the prediction error, in both directions.

The loss has a trivial minimum: map every image to the same vector and the error is zero. This is collapse. Every JEPA needs a second ingredient to stop it. The study compares eight:

  • EMA target: view 2’s embedding comes from a slowly updated copy of the encoder, and no gradient flows through it.
  • VICReg (Bardes et al. 2022): penalises embedding dimensions whose spread is too small, and correlations between dimensions. It names no target distribution.
  • SIGReg (Balestriero & LeCun 2025): pushes random one-dimensional projections of the batch toward a standard normal.
  • KSD: the kernel Stein discrepancy (Liu et al. 2016) measures how far a batch is from a target density using only the gradient of the target’s log-density. Here the kernel is inverse multiquadric (Gorham & Mackey 2017) and the target is .
  • Sliced KSD (Gong et al. 2021): KSD along random directions.
  • MMD: compares the batch with a fresh sample from through kernel averages.
  • Oracle: KSD toward a target that knows the content dimension : six full-size dimensions, the rest shrunk.
  • None: no regulariser. It collapses in 100% of seeds.

All regularised arms add one term, weighted by , to the prediction loss. SIGReg, KSD, sliced KSD and MMD all aim at an isotropic Gaussian.

2 Data

2.1 3DShapes

  • Source. 3DShapes (Burgess & Kim 2018) is a DeepMind dataset of 480,000 rendered 64×64 images. Each shows one object in a room, at every combination of six factors: floor hue, wall hue, object hue, object scale, object shape and orientation.
  • Motive. It was built to test whether a model recovers known generating factors.
  • Use here. The six factors split into two groups:
    • content, shared by both views: object hue, scale and shape, coded as numbers;
    • nuisance, which may differ between views: floor hue, wall hue and orientation.
  • Views. Two images share content. Each nuisance factor is redrawn with probability , and light pixel noise is added. At the views differ only by pixel noise.
  • Why the method fits. All six factors are recorded for every image, so a probe can be aimed at the nuisance and nothing else.
  • Cost of a wrong answer. A practitioner who blames the target distribution for leakage would swap regularisers when the fix is a weight or a width.

2.2 Other tiers

  • Temporal clips. Three-frame 3DShapes clips in which nuisance factors drift one step per frame with probability . The model predicts frame 3’s embedding from frames 1 and 2.
  • Autoencoders. A β-VAE (Higgins et al. 2017) and KSD and MMD autoencoders at the same . They reconstruct pixels, so they serve as a reference for models that must keep everything.
  • CIFAR-10. CIFAR-10 (Krizhevsky 2009) is 60,000 labelled 32×32 photographs in 10 classes, built as a classification benchmark. Its nuisance is the augmentation parameters (crop box, flip, colour jitter), known because the pipeline draws them.

3 Leakage

Leakage asks whether the ignored factors can still be read off the trained embedding:

  • Freeze the encoder.
  • Embed 10,000 training-split images and fit a linear regression from embedding to nuisance factors.
  • Score on 5,000 images from a held-out 10% of factor combinations.

That is the leakage. Zero means the nuisance is not linearly readable; one means it is fully readable. The same probe aimed at the content factors gives content . A good encoder has high content and low leakage.

A k-nearest-neighbour probe (10 neighbours) gives a second, nonlinear leakage score. On photographs neither probe has a target, because the list of what differs between two views is unknown.

4 Protocol

  • Encoder. A small convolutional network with no normalisation layers, . The base setting is , , .
  • Training. 2000 steps, batch of 256 pairs.
  • Tuning. Every arm gets three levels of (×1/5, ×1, ×5 around a pilot value), or three EMA decay rates. The level with the highest content on two tuning seeds wins. Leakage never enters the choice.
  • Evaluation. 5 fresh seeds per configuration, 95% bootstrap intervals over seeds.
  • Size. 495 held-out runs, 747 runs in total including tuning.

5 Regulariser strength

The first hypothesis was about the target law. A regulariser that pushes toward an isotropic Gaussian must spread variance over all dimensions; with , the spare dimensions have nothing to hold but nuisance. So Gaussian-target arms should leak more than VICReg and EMA.

At the tuned and , the opposite holds. Linear leakage, mean [95% interval]:

  • VICReg: 0.673 [0.542, 0.772]
  • SIGReg: 0.250 [0.218, 0.281]
  • EMA: 0.215 [0.137, 0.283]
  • sliced KSD: 0.019 [0.008, 0.029]
  • MMD: 0.012 [0.000, 0.026]
  • KSD: 0.002 [−0.001, 0.005]

At and , 8 of 8 Gaussian-arm minus VICReg contrasts are negative with intervals that exclude zero.

The ranking does not survive a change of . Rerunning every regulariser at all three of its levels on the held-out seeds gives leakage at the highest minus leakage at the lowest:

  • VICReg: +0.499 [0.349, 0.596]
  • SIGReg: +0.370 [0.272, 0.467]
  • sliced KSD: +0.522 [0.427, 0.588]
  • KSD: +0.532 [0.458, 0.602]
  • MMD: +0.333 [0.215, 0.449]
  • oracle: +0.493 [0.382, 0.575]

What the six contrasts show:

  • All six are positive, with intervals that exclude zero.
  • VICReg names no target distribution and still follows the pattern.
  • At five times its tuned , KSD leaks more than VICReg at VICReg’s least-leaky level (+0.210 [0.146, 0.266]).
  • Pushing harder costs content: KSD’s content falls from 0.727 at its tuned to 0.340 at 25 times it.
  • The VICReg baseline itself depends on the choice. Tuning picked VICReg’s middle level, which leaks as much as its highest (0.673 against 0.671, and 0.172 at the lowest); against VICReg’s least-leaky level, the tuned SIGReg leaks more (+0.078 [0.032, 0.120]), which is the direction the hypothesis predicted.

More distributional pressure buys more leakage, whatever the target. Tuning for content picked low-pressure levels for the KSD family and a high-leakage level for VICReg, and those choices, not the Gaussian target, decide the comparison.

5.1 λ explorer

The chart shows linear leakage and linear content on the held-out seeds against divided by the tuned (log scale; dotted line = tuned). Bars are 95% intervals.

  • Compare each arm’s lowest and highest : leakage is higher at the highest for every arm.
  • Content at the highest is lower than at the tuned for every arm.
  • KSD and sliced KSD were tuned at the bottom of their grids, so their curves start at 1.

6 Embedding width and noise

There are two obvious ways to squeeze an embedding so it cannot carry everything:

  • Width: give it fewer dimensions, a lower .
  • Information bottleneck: add Gaussian noise of size to the embedding before the predictor sees it, which limits how much detail gets through. The noise is scaled to the batch spread of the embedding, so the encoder cannot escape it by growing its outputs. Probes read the clean embedding.

The hypothesis was that noise removes nuisance where width does not. The data say the reverse. Contrasts at , mean [95% interval]:

  • Narrowing from 24 to 6 lowers linear leakage for all six arms.
  • Narrowing also lowers content for all six. Width is a trade, not a free filter.
  • Raising from 0 to 1 lowers content for all six, and raises leakage for all except VICReg, whose change is not distinguishable from zero.
  • EMA’s kNN leakage does fall with noise (−0.107 [−0.153, −0.060]), but its content falls with it. Its embedding is degrading, not filtering.

Shrinking spare dimensions is not the same as removing them. The oracle arm squeezes its spare dimensions toward zero, yet leaks 0.451 at and 0.685 at . The probe standardises every dimension first, so a small dimension reads as clearly as a large one.

6.1 Configuration explorer

The chart shows linear leakage and content (mean, 95% interval over 5 seeds) at the tuned . The study ran three slices through the base setting, not a full grid:

  • at , , all eight arms;
  • at , , six arms (no oracle, no “none”);
  • at , , the same six arms.

Other combinations show “not run”. Nothing is interpolated.

Things to try:

  • Set , and compare with : linear leakage is higher at for every arm except the collapsed “none” baseline. EMA and MMD collapsed in some seeds at , so part of their low leakage there is collapse; the table counts the seeds.
  • Set and or , then compare with : leakage is higher at for every arm except VICReg, and content is lower for every arm.
  • Set , and compare with : leakage is lower at for every arm, though VICReg’s change is not distinguishable from zero. When the nuisance never changes between views, nothing pushes the encoder to drop it.
  • Turn on kNN leakage at the base setting: KSD, sliced KSD and MMD hold nuisance a linear probe cannot read.

7 Other results

  • Matched priors (identifiability = how well a rotation and scaling of the embedding recovers the content factors). When the content factors follow a non-Gaussian law, KSD toward a matched prior does not beat KSD toward .
    • Uniform law: matched 0.554 [0.501, 0.598] vs Gaussian target 0.576 [0.543, 0.595].
    • Laplace law: matched 0.276 [0.235, 0.317] vs Gaussian target 0.772 [0.717, 0.813].
  • EMA under nuisance. EMA’s leakage falls with , as every regulariser’s does. The size of its drop matches KSD’s (difference: −0.048 [−0.161, 0.055]) and sliced KSD’s, and is larger than VICReg’s (−0.417 [−0.563, −0.260]), SIGReg’s and MMD’s. Its geometry differs: effective rank (roughly, how many dimensions the embedding uses) is 4.0 for EMA against 11.0 for SIGReg.
  • Temporal clips. EMA alone leaks 0.484 [0.381, 0.601], sliced KSD alone 0.098 [0.033, 0.164]. Adding sliced KSD to EMA raises leakage by +0.229 [0.110, 0.337].
  • Autoencoders. β-VAE, KSD-AE and MMD-AE leak 0.809, 0.912 and 0.855. 21 of 21 autoencoder minus JEPA contrasts are positive; the smallest is β-VAE − VICReg, +0.136 [0.028, 0.267].
  • CIFAR-10. Augmentation leakage is small for every arm, from 0.018 (KSD) to 0.049 (EMA). KSD has the best linear class accuracy, 0.357 [0.350, 0.365].

8 Constraints

  • One small rendered world. A small convolutional encoder, 2000 steps, rendered scenes downsampled to 32×32. Large encoders on photographs may behave differently; the CIFAR-10 tier is a single slice.
  • λ tuned once. Levels were chosen at the base setting and reused for the , and slices, so part of the width and noise effects may come from a that is no longer the best there. Several arms, KSD and sliced KSD included, were tuned at the lowest of their grids.
  • Linear leakage is the headline. Low linear leakage is not absence of nuisance: KSD’s kNN leakage at the base setting is 0.191 [0.172, 0.213] against linear 0.002, and SIGReg’s kNN leakage exceeds EMA’s (+0.158 [0.094, 0.217]).
  • One kind of noise. is noise on the predictor input. Other information bottlenecks were not tested.
  • Collapse at . EMA and MMD collapsed in some seeds at ; the explorer table lists the count.
  • Five seeds. Intervals are percentile bootstraps over 5 unpaired seeds. Read intervals that just touch zero as weak.

Pressure. Buys. Leakage. Width. Filters. Nuisance. Noise. Hurts. Targets. Matter. Less.

9 References

  • Assran, M. et al. (2023). Self-Supervised Learning From Images With a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture. CVPR, pp. 15619–15629.
  • Balestriero, R. & LeCun, Y. (2025). LeJEPA: Provable and Scalable Self-Supervised Learning Without the Heuristics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08544
  • Bardes, A., Ponce, J. & LeCun, Y. (2022). VICReg: Variance-Invariance-Covariance Regularization for Self-Supervised Learning. ICLR. https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.04906
  • Burgess, C. & Kim, H. (2018). 3D Shapes Dataset. DeepMind. https://github.com/deepmind/3dshapes-dataset/
  • Gong, W., Li, Y. & Hernández-Lobato, J. M. (2021). Sliced Kernelized Stein Discrepancy. ICLR. https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16531
  • Gorham, J. & Mackey, L. (2017). Measuring Sample Quality with Kernels. ICML. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/gorham17a.html
  • Higgins, I. et al. (2017). β-VAE: Learning Basic Visual Concepts with a Constrained Variational Framework. ICLR. https://openreview.net/pdf?id=Sy2fzU9gl
  • Krizhevsky, A. (2009). Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images. Technical report. https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~kriz/cifar.html
  • Liu, Q., Lee, J. & Jordan, M. (2016). A Kernelized Stein Discrepancy for Goodness-of-fit Tests. ICML. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v48/liub16.html

item.title: The Thermodynamics of Logistic Regression: Bridging Energy Landscapes, Cross-Entropy, and Probit Models
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
A binary classifier’s probability can be derived from an energy gap, fitted by an information cost, or obtained by adding noise to a threshold. These three descriptions agree for logistic regression, while the choice of latent noise explains where probit regression differs.

1 Physics: a two-state energy model

Fix an input and a label . Let . Give the two states dimensionless energies

Only their difference affects the probabilities. In the chosen energy gauge,

At inverse temperature , the partition function sums the two Boltzmann weights:

Normalizing the weight of state 1 gives the logistic sigmoid, step by step:

Thus : the linear score is the log odds and the energy gap. If we restore , the sigmoid takes as its argument. Temperature rescales the coefficients; ordinary logistic regression fixes that scale at one.

The conditional Helmholtz free energy in these units is . The zero of energy is arbitrary: adding the same to both state energies changes by but leaves the energy gap and probabilities fixed. Statistical mechanics derives these relations from the canonical ensemble.

The two states are the possible labels at one fixed input, not two positions that moves between. A physical counterpart is a spin that can point in two directions while an external field is held fixed: the field changes the energy gap, and thermal equilibrium favors the lower-energy direction. Here sets the field through , and choosing a label corresponds to choosing a spin direction. No motion between states or heat flow is modeled. The classifier’s energies are dimensionless scores unless a physical system supplies an energy scale and temperature; alone does not measure a real temperature.

1.1 An energy surface to adjust

The display uses ten synthetic feature pairs, chosen to put both labels on either side of a linear boundary. They stand in for two standardized measurements in a binary classification task; no observed population or sampling claim is attached. A wrong classification would assign high probability to the opposite state, and the two-state model is a useful controlled example because its energy gap is visible directly.

The colored plane is ; the faint horizontal plane is . Class-1 points sit on the colored plane and class-0 points sit on the zero-energy plane. Stems show the gap between the two possible label energies at a fixed input. Lower energy means higher Boltzmann probability. A linear plane has lower-energy regions, not local wells or peaks.

  1. Increase : the colored plane tilts down as increases, lowering the class-1 energy there.
  2. Increase : the entire class-1 plane drops while the class-0 plane stays at zero; for , rises at every point.
  3. Change inverse temperature : the energy planes stay in place while the probability at the highlighted input becomes sharper or flatter. At , both labels have probability everywhere, so the drawn zero-gap line is no longer the only equal-probability location.
  4. Drag to orbit. For , the intersection of the two planes is the boundary.

2 Information: likelihood, surprise, and cross-entropy

The Boltzmann probability becomes a training rule when we observe labeled pairs . Write and . Conditional independence gives the Bernoulli likelihood

Taking logs turns the product into a sum. Maximum likelihood therefore minimizes the average negative log-likelihood:

The first line is binary cross-entropy (BCE). The per-example value is the observed label’s surprisal, measured in nats. The last line shows the physical terms: lower observed-state energy helps, while the log partition function charges for assigning weight to both possible states. The standard log-loss definition is this negative log-likelihood.

The KL statement needs its empirical distribution stated. For a particular training pair, let , a point mass on the observed label. Since ,

If an input has repeated observations and an empirical class frequency , then . Its entropy does not depend on , so minimizing cross-entropy and KL still gives the same fit. This is a statement about the observed conditional frequencies; it does not say that an arbitrary finite sample recovers the population distribution.

Training adjusts the gap so observed labels occupy lower-energy states more often. The resulting change in follows from the normalization.

2.1 A loss surface to adjust

The second view plots mean BCE for the same ten synthetic observations over while holding fixed and using . Its height is an average surprisal in nats, not a physical energy. The marked point is the current pair of coefficients. Change either weight to move the point on the surface; change to change the entire surface. These ten labels are linearly separable, so increasing the coefficient magnitudes along a separating direction keeps lowering BCE. Flip the highlighted observation’s label to introduce a conflict and bend the loss surface toward a finite minimum. The loss readout also works when the 3D scene cannot load.

2.2 Joint distribution of inputs and labels

The energy calculation normalizes over at fixed . BCE likewise scores labels conditional on the observed inputs. Logistic regression therefore specifies , but leaves the distribution of inputs unspecified. If we separately choose a marginal density or mass function , then

Different choices of give the same logistic conditional probabilities but different joint distributions, and can change the class balance and feature distributions within each class . In particular, logistic does not imply Gaussian ; a generative model such as Gaussian discriminant analysis adds assumptions about the feature distributions. Stanford’s CS229 notes distinguish these directions.

This also limits the physical picture. is a conditional partition function, not a normalizer over all . A joint Boltzmann model needs an input measure or reference energy. If the raw weights were integrable over , they would imply a feature marginal proportional to ; with the chosen gauge on , the integral is infinite. The plotted planes compare labels at each input, not the frequency or physical energy of input locations. A population average of BCE weights conditional errors by how often occurs, but fitting BCE does not fit that input distribution.

3 Statistics: latent noise and the probit link

The same classifier can be built as a noisy threshold. Let

For a symmetric error distribution with cumulative distribution function ,

  • Logit: has a standard logistic distribution, . An equivalent random-utility construction adds independent Gumbel errors to the two state utilities and compares them; their difference is logistic. A derivation of the Gumbel difference gives the same choice probability.
  • Probit: , so , the standard normal CDF. This is the probit link. With a normal error of standard deviation , the argument is .

The normal density can be written as with harmonic potential . This potential belongs to the latent noise, not to the two-label energy surface in the first section. Probit and logit share a linear decision boundary at , but their probability tails differ:

The logistic tail is heavier than the Gaussian tail; both decay faster than any power law. Coefficient scales must be matched before comparing curves, since standard logistic noise has variance and standard normal noise has variance .

3.1 Tail decay and optimization

For a positive observation, the derivative of negative log-likelihood with respect to the score is

When , both gradients vanish, but the probit gradient vanishes on a Gaussian scale. When a positive label is assigned a large negative score, the logit gradient approaches , while the probit gradient grows approximately as . A confidently wrong or mislabeled example can therefore exert more gradient pressure under probit; logit’s bounded score gradient can be less sensitive to such extremes. This comparison concerns the gradient with respect to ; the parameter gradient also multiplies , so neither model is automatically robust to high-leverage feature outliers.

4 Concept map

Physics Information theory Binary classification
Energy gap Log odds Linear score
Boltzmann weight Probability assigned to a state Bernoulli class probability
Partition function Normalization inside surprisal Log-sum-exp term in BCE
Surprisal Per-example negative log-likelihood
Changing the energy gap Reducing conditional cross-entropy and KL Fitting by maximum likelihood
Holding fixed BCE scores A joint also needs a marginal
Harmonic energy of Gaussian latent noise Faster tail decay Probit probability

Energies. Normalize. Probabilities. Observe. Surprise. Fit. Noise. Changes. Tails. Matter.

5 References

  • Rutgers University, Statistical Mechanics, chapter 3 — canonical probabilities, partition functions, and free energy.
  • Scikit-learn, log_loss documentation — Bernoulli negative log-likelihood and cross-entropy.
  • Stanford, Learning and Inference via Maximum Inner Product Search — Gumbel noise differences and logistic choice probabilities.
  • Statsmodels, Probit link documentation — the normal-CDF response function.
  • Stanford CS229, Generative Learning Algorithms — discriminative and generative models and the limits of the logistic conditional form.

item.title: Code Review at Agent Speed
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
When agents write most of the code, nobody can read every line before it merges, so code review has to become a stack of checks, each aimed at a different way a change can go wrong. The Claude Code team at Anthropic runs seven such layers, and an ordinary GitHub repository can set up a version of every one of them today.

1 The review bottleneck

Anyone who has reviewed code for long has approved a pull request without really reading it. The diff runs to six hundred lines, the tests are green, the author has been right before, and a meeting starts in four minutes. We scroll to the bottom and type “LGTM”.

The odd part is what that approval records. The green tick says a person checked the change. What the person mostly checked is that the tests ran.

Anthropic has a number that hints at the size of that gap. Before it built an automated reviewer, only 16% of its pull requests received substantive review comments (Anthropic, 2026a). By its own account, many got skims rather than deep reads. Line-by-line review was already a skim, and it was a skim at human speed.

Agents take away the speed limit. Anthropic’s monorepo landed about 2,500 changes a day in May 2026 and more than 30,000 a day by September (Anthropic, 2026b). The engineers who reported that number opened their post with the sentence that sums up the shift: “At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research.”

A rough calculation shows why reading cannot keep up. Suppose a careful review takes 15 minutes, a figure picked for illustration rather than measured. Then 30,000 changes a day need 7,500 reviewer-hours a day: the working days of about 940 full-time reviewers.

Line-by-line review breaks in three places once agents write the code:

  • Volume. Reviewers scale with headcount. Changes now scale with compute.
  • False assurance. A skim is a check with large holes that looks like a thorough one, so nobody adds the checks that would cover the holes.
  • Noise. An agent author acts on every comment. A nit that a person would wave away becomes a commit, and the commit needs another review.
Two repositories, two numbers

The 30,000-a-day figure is Anthropic’s monorepo. Claude Code lives in a separate repository. There, Claude writes about 90% of the code, and merged pull requests more than doubled from June to September 2026 (Osmani, Lunt and Wang, 2026).

The Claude Code team’s response was to keep review and change its shape (Osmani, Lunt and Wang, 2026):

We didn’t remove review. But we did move most of the reading to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes.

In the same June-to-September stretch, the share of merged pull requests that had to be reverted fell by more than 40%. A revert is a change undone after it landed. A falling share means fewer bad merges per merge, during months when merges more than doubled.

2 What review is for

Code review has always done two jobs. It finds and fixes problems before they ship, and it spreads knowledge of the codebase through the team, since reading a colleague’s diff is how most of us learn what changed and how the pieces fit.

The first job is where the Claude Code team changed the question. In their words:

We think “did a human read the code?” is an imprecise proxy for “what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?”

The new question names a failure first and a check second. A type error belongs to the type checker. Two pull requests that pass alone and break together belong to a merge queue. A feature nobody should have built belongs to a person, because no test can say whether the product needs it.

Safety engineering has a picture for this way of thinking. Every defence has gaps: a checklist gets skipped, an alarm is silenced, a second pilot is tired. An accident needs the gaps in several defences to line up at once. James Reason drew the defences as slices of Swiss cheese whose holes sit in different places, and the drawing is now called the Swiss cheese model (Reason, 2000). The cover image is one version of it.

The Claude Code team’s own diagram of its process is the same picture: six layers of checks with holes in different places, and fast rollback underneath to catch what falls through all six. The model changes what “better review” means. A thicker slice helps less than another slice with holes somewhere else, and line-by-line human review was one slice with holes wherever a tired reader’s attention lapsed.

Moving the reading to machines also moved review earlier. Review used to be a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for a colleague. The team now describes it this way:

Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write.

The goal they set is specific. Most pull requests to the Claude Code repositories — the CLI, the desktop and web apps, and the mobile apps — should merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no rise in reverts or incidents. Four numbers track it:

  • human approvals per PR, at the median and at the 95th percentile (the PR that needs more approvals than 95% of the others)
  • human comments per PR
  • how long a PR waits on a person
  • revert and incident rates, as the guardrail

The guardrail exists because review time saved can come back as repair time: “if they rise, we haven’t saved human time, we’ve only moved it.”

Figure 1 traces a typical change from the author’s machine to users.

3 The seven layers

The source numbers seven layers. The table lists what each is for and whether it can stop a merge.

# Layer Aimed at Stops a merge
1 Verification before the PR broken builds, failing tests, behaviour the author’s agent can observe runs before a PR exists
