What lies beneath the waterline, in his view, is the brain’s own spatiotemporal structure: a hierarchy of timescale priors that feeds continuously into the predicting self before a single task or thought gets underway.

Every cortical rung listens through a different window

Tap a guitar string in a dry closet and the note dies in a fraction of a second; tap it in a cathedral and the room holds the tone for seconds. Before any melody is played, the room already has an opinion about how long an event lasts.

Cortical circuits differ in the same way even when nothing much is happening. Record from a patch of cortex at rest, compare its activity at one moment with its activity a short lag later, and the correlation drops off roughly as an exponential, . That decay constant is what Northoff and colleagues call an intrinsic neural timescale (and what John Murray’s macaque recordings mapped across the cortical sheet): the length of the window over which a neural population naturally pools its own recent past.

Those windows are not uniform across the brain; they form a steep gradient. Primary sensory areas — visual, auditory, somatosensory cortex — run fast clocks, with in the tens of milliseconds, because a circuit that lingered on the last phoneme would blur the next one. Climb up through association cortex toward transmodal hubs and the default mode network — the regions most consistently tied to self-referential thought and autobiographical continuity — and stretches into hundreds of milliseconds and beyond. Each rung listens to the world through a window of a different width, which raises a mechanical question: what happens when a hierarchy of windows like that is wired into Friston’s prediction loop?

Slow windows act as priors that refuse to flicker

In active inference, every rung of the cortical hierarchy passes top-down predictions to the rung beneath it and receives bottom-up prediction errors in return. How much a rung moves when an error arrives depends on a prior over rate of change: if a level assumes its hidden cause changes slowly, a brief spike of error is treated as local weather rather than a shift in climate. Northoff’s intrinsic timescales turn that abstract prior into hardware. A rung with a long window physically averages over dozens of fast cycles from the rung beneath it, so only errors that persist on the slow rung’s own timescale can bend its state.

To see the two timescales pull apart, the interactive simulation generates a synthetic sensory stream sampled every . The stream combines a slow sinusoidal baseline (standing in for an ongoing bodily and situational state), seeded zero-mean Gaussian noise (standing in for rapid sensory fluctuations), and a surprise burst starting at (standing in for a sudden transient disturbance like the horn on the street). We use a synthetic two-filter model here so the true underlying baseline and the isolated deflection from the burst are known at every millisecond; if a slow rung chased the raw noise in a real brain, the self-model would jitter with every saccade and acoustic edge. Two leaky integrators read that stream in parallel: a fast sensory rung fixed at , and a slow prior rung whose timescale we can step from up to .

At the default setting (, sharp burst of ), the slow prior’s autocorrelation half-life is , only of the fast sensory noise passes into the slow state, and the -unit surprise burst deflects the slow state by a peak of . Step down to so the slow rung matches the sensory clock: the half-life drops to , passed noise jumps to , and the burst yanks the state by units — the two traces collapse onto each other and the baseline is lost in the spike. Now step up through (half-life , noise , peak deflection ) to : the half-life reaches , passed noise falls to , and the burst moves the slow state by just . Toggling the surprise burst to moderate () or none () at lowers the peak deflection to and while the noise floor stays fixed.

That gap between the dashed sensory trace ( units of deflection at ) and the solid slow trace ( units at ) is what a hierarchy of timescale priors buys. The fast rung has to be jumpy so you do not step in front of the car; the slow rung has to be stubborn so the person stepping back on the kerb is still the person who left the house five minutes ago. Even so, a stubborn filter only explains so much.

Caveat: a slow clock is not yet a someone

A leaky integrator with is five lines of arithmetic, and nobody thinks a low-pass filter on a circuit board has an inner life. Northoff’s hierarchy of intrinsic timescales explains why a self-model has temporal thickness — why the predictor’s estimate of itself spans seconds and scenes rather than resetting every forty milliseconds — just as recursive prediction explains why the boundary between self and world falls where action has reliable control. Neither mechanism, on its own, explains why that temporally thick model feels like anything from the inside. What the timescale hierarchy does settle is a constraint: whatever accounts for subjective continuity cannot be built out of fast clocks alone.

The water holds the tip up

Return to Northoff’s iceberg from that conversation in Bogotá. Friston’s free energy principle gives the calculus at the waterline — predictions flowing down, errors flowing up, action and perception trading off to keep surprise low. Underneath that calculus sits a physical commitment to time: a nested stack of integration windows, widening from tens of milliseconds at the sensory rim to hundreds of milliseconds and seconds in the networks that track the organism itself. Without those slow priors underneath the sea, a predictive brain would still correct its errors frame by frame, but it could never pool enough frames together to notice the one thing that never leaves the room.

Fast. Senses. Flicker. Slow. Priors. Pool. Errors. Fade. Selves. Endure.

References

  • Georg Northoff on spatiotemporal neuroscience and intrinsic neural timescales (The Spontaneous Brain, MIT Press).
  • Karl Friston on the free energy principle, active inference, and hierarchical temporal scales in cortex.
  • John D. Murray et al. (2014), “A hierarchy of intrinsic timescales across primate cortex,” Nature Neuroscience.
  • The One Thing Always in the Room — the companion essay on recursive prediction and the self as an invariant.

item.title: How to Read a Paper in the Age of AI
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
The classic guides to reading a research paper were written before an AI assistant could summarize, explain or critique one. Their advice still holds: read in layers, with a goal, and verify by reconstruction. What has changed is that AI can now do the first layer for you, tutor you through the second, and argue with you after the third.

The field-specific guides (mathematics, statistics, CS, computational biology, neuroscience) change what you read closely, not the layers. The evidence on AI tools, on how researchers use them, and on where they fail points to one protocol: AI before and after your own reading, not instead of it.

A 20-minute slide version of this post, for a lab meeting or journal club, steps through the passes on a 3D model of a paper.

1 The classics: general guides

Every good guide agrees on one thing: a paper is not read front to back, once. You read it in layers, with a goal set before you start.

General guides to reading a paper.
Guide Year Core idea Best for
Keshav, “How to Read a Paper” 2007 Three passes. Pass 1 (5–10 min): title, abstract, intro, headings, conclusions; answer the “five Cs” (category, context, correctness, contributions, clarity). Pass 2 (~1 h): figures and argument, skip proofs. Pass 3: virtually re-implement the work. Also a recipe for a literature survey. CS, systems, any conference/arXiv paper
Carey, Steiner & Petri, “Ten simple rules for reading a scientific paper” (PLOS Comp Bio) 2020 Pick a reading goal first; read the figures before the text; question each panel; afterwards ask “now what?” and connect it to your own science. Biology, comp bio, students and mentors
Mensh & Kording, “Ten simple rules for structuring papers” (PLOS Comp Bio) 2017 A writing guide, but its context–content–conclusion model tells a reader where each claim lives in a well-built paper. Neuroscience, comp bio
Leek group guide to reading papers 2016 A working statistician’s own process, kept as an open GitHub guide; pairs with his guides to reviewing papers. Statistics, genomics, data science

Keshav’s method is the shared skeleton. The later guides mostly change what you read on each pass (figures in biology, theorems in mathematics, data and design in statistics), not the layered structure.

2 Field-specific guides

Each field shifts the unit of attention: theorems in mathematics, design and inference in statistics, claims-versus-evidence in CS, figures and data in biology, analysis pitfalls in neuroscience.

2.1 Mathematics

  • Simonson & Gouvêa, “How to Read Mathematics”: mathematics has its own “reading protocol”; read slowly, keep the big picture, test every claim with an example, make the idea your own.
  • Petra Schwer, “How to Read Mathematics?” (arXiv 2607.24136, 2026): a recent study guide. Read in hours per page, not pages per hour; for proofs, skim for the idea, go line by line, then summarize. It also warns against leaning on AI to do the reasoning for you.
  • Tanya Khovanova, “How to Read a Math Paper” (2026): match the reading to the goal. To learn a paper deeply, iterate up to six reads: structure, definitions, statements with small examples, proof ideas, the references, then reproduce the proofs yourself.
  • MathComm’s reading-mathematics list: links Lara Alcock’s research on how experts and novices read proofs, Reiter’s question lists, and Matt Baker’s “How to Read a Research Paper”.

2.2 Statistics and biostatistics

  • Greenhalgh, How to Read a Paper (BMJ series 1997; book now in its 6th edition): the standard critical-appraisal text. Its two “Statistics for the non-statistician” chapters (part II on significance pitfalls) are a checklist for any applied-statistics paper.
  • Leek group guide to reading papers and the Leek genomics paper list: how a statistical genomicist reads, plus a curated canon to read.
  • Reader’s checklist for statistical claims: what is the estimand (the quantity the study sets out to estimate); is the design causal or observational; how many comparisons were made; is the effect size reported with uncertainty; are code and data available.

2.3 Computer science and machine learning

  • Keshav’s three passes remain the default for systems and conference papers.
  • Andrew Ng’s Stanford CS230 talk on reading papers (2019): read a field as a list of papers, skimming many and going deep on a few; about 5–20 papers for working knowledge, 50–100 for depth; re-derive the math and re-run the code.
  • For ML papers specifically: check baselines, compute budgets, ablations, seeds, and whether the benchmark is contaminated.

2.4 Computational biology

  • Carey et al. (2020): read the figures first and interrogate each panel.
  • Add the computational layer: is the code public and runnable; which reference versions, parameters and thresholds were used; would the result survive a different pipeline.

2.5 Neuroscience

There is no single canonical neuroscience guide; the field’s best reading aids are its methods-critique papers, used as checklists:

  • Mensh & Kording (2017) on where claims live in a paper.
  • Known traps to check for: low statistical power, “double dipping” (selecting and testing on the same data), and comparing two significance tests instead of testing the interaction directly.
  • Practical course guides such as Case Western’s NeuroWiki and this cognitive-neuroscience primer.

3 The AI tool landscape for reading papers

AI tools now cover every stage Keshav describes, from finding papers to interrogating a single equation. They are strongest at triage and navigation, weakest at judging whether a result is right.

AI tools by the job they do.
Job What the tools do Examples Main caveat
Discover and map a field Semantic search, citation graphs, “papers like this one” Semantic Scholar, Connected Papers, ResearchRabbit, Undermind Coverage gaps; ranking favors highly cited work
Synthesize many papers Retrieval-augmented answers with citations; “deep research” agents Elicit, Consensus, OpenScholar, PaperQA2, ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini research modes Fabricated or mismatched citations; overgeneralized claims
Read one paper with help Chat with the PDF, explain a figure, define a term inline, summarize a section alphaXiv, Semantic Reader, SciSpace, NotebookLM, general chat assistants Summaries flatten caveats and hedges
Check citation context Shows whether later work supports or disputes a claim scite Classifier errors on nuanced citations
Verify math and code Re-derive steps, check a proof sketch, re-run or port code General assistants with code execution; proof assistants (Lean) for formal checks Confident but wrong derivations unless formally checked

The most rigorous evidence so far is for retrieval-grounded systems. OpenScholar, published in Nature in February 2026, answers questions from a store of 45 million open-access papers. In its tests a general model (GPT-4o) fabricated citations roughly 78–90% of the time, while OpenScholar’s citation accuracy approached that of human experts, and experts preferred its answers over expert-written ones about 50–70% of the time.

The practical lesson: use tools that retrieve and cite real documents, and click through every citation that matters. Product rankings in this space change monthly; independent roundups like this 2026 comparison are a starting point, not a verdict.

4 How researchers use AI to read

AI-assisted reading is now mainstream, and it is moving fastest in peer review, where reading closely is the job.

  • Peer reviewers. A Frontiers survey of about 1,600 researchers (reported January 2026) found over half now use AI when reviewing, up from 24% in 2024. Use runs higher among early-career researchers (61%) than senior ones (45%), and varies by region (77% in China, 31% in North America). The top uses were writing the report (59%), summarizing the article’s findings (29%) and flagging possible misconduct (28%).
  • Researchers broadly. Wiley’s ExplanAItions study of almost 5,000 researchers (2025) found use still fairly narrow in tools and tasks, with 63% citing unclear guidelines or lack of training as barriers.
  • Common workflows that have emerged:
    • Triage at scale: ask an assistant for the five Cs of each of 30 candidate papers, then pick five to read yourself.
    • Tutor on demand: paste an unfamiliar method section and ask for the prerequisites, a worked toy example, or the notation decoded.
    • Adversarial second reader: after your own pass, ask the model to list the weakest assumption, missing controls or alternative explanations, then judge those yourself.
    • Reproduction partner: have it help re-implement an analysis or re-derive an equation, which turns Keshav’s “virtual re-implementation” into a literal one.

The pattern that holds up: AI before and after your own reading, not instead of it.

5 Risks and pitfalls

The three failure modes to plan around are distorted summaries, invented sources, and the slow loss of your own reading skill.

Risks of AI-assisted reading.
Risk Evidence What to do
Summaries overstate findings Peters & Chin-Yee (Royal Society Open Science, 2025) tested 10 models on 4,900 summaries. Model summaries of medical papers were nearly 5 times likelier to overgeneralize than expert-written ones; some newer models were worse, and asking to “avoid inaccuracies” made it worse still. Read the abstract’s hedges and the limitations section yourself. Ask the model to quote the exact sentence behind each claim.
Fabricated or mismatched citations General models invented most citations in the OpenScholar tests. Use retrieval-grounded tools; open every citation you will rely on or repeat.
Deskilling and shallow understanding MIT’s “Your Brain on ChatGPT” preprint (small sample, essay writing) found lower neural engagement and weaker recall in the LLM-assisted group. Schwer’s 2026 math reading guide warns of the same trade-off. Do the first pass and the hard parts (proofs, derivations, figure reading) unaided; use AI to check, not to replace, that work.
Confidentiality Uploading an unpublished manuscript you are reviewing may breach journal policy. Check the journal’s AI policy before using any tool on a manuscript under review.

6 A protocol: the three passes, updated for AI

Keep Keshav’s structure, add an AI-assisted pass zero and a verification pass, and keep the judgment passes yours.

  1. Pass 0, triage (AI-led, ~2 min per paper). Use a retrieval-grounded tool to find candidates and get each one’s five Cs. Set your reading goal (Carey et al., Rule 1) before going further.
  2. Pass 1, the bird’s-eye view (you, 5–10 min). Title, abstract, intro, headings, conclusion, and every figure. Write your own one-sentence summary before reading any AI summary, then compare the two.
  3. Pass 2, the argument (you, with AI as tutor, ~1 h). Read the main text and figures. Ask AI to unpack unfamiliar methods, notation or prerequisites, with toy examples. Note each claim and its supporting evidence.
  4. Pass 3, the field-specific deep read (you, hours).
    • Math: work small examples; re-prove the key lemma; formalize one step if it matters.
    • Statistics: identify the estimand, design and multiplicity; re-run the analysis if data exist.
    • CS and ML: check baselines, ablations and compute; re-implement the core method.
    • Comp bio: run the pipeline, or at least audit versions and parameters.
    • Neuroscience: check power, circular analysis and interaction tests.
  5. Pass 4, adversarial check (AI as skeptic, then you). Ask for the weakest assumption, missing controls and alternative explanations; demand quoted evidence from the paper. Verify any citation you will rely on.
  6. Integrate (you). Write a short note in your own words: what it claims, how far you believe it, and what you would do next.

Read. In. Layers. AI. Triages. Tutors. Argues. You. Judge.

References

Reading guides

  • Keshav, How to Read a Paper (2007)
  • Carey, Steiner & Petri, Ten simple rules for reading a scientific paper (2020)
  • Mensh & Kording, Ten simple rules for structuring papers (2017)
  • Leek group guide to reading papers
  • Schwer, How to Read Mathematics? (2026)
  • Khovanova, How to Read a Math Paper (2026)
  • MathComm: Reading mathematics resources
  • Greenhalgh, How to Read a Paper (6th ed.)
  • Andrew Ng on reading research papers (KDnuggets)

AI and reading

  • OpenScholar in Nature (Nature Asia press release)
  • Peters & Chin-Yee on overgeneralization (PsyPost)
  • Frontiers survey on AI in peer review (NISO)
  • Wiley ExplanAItions study (NISO)
  • Your Brain on ChatGPT (MIT Media Lab)

item.title: AlphaTensor, Part 3: A Game Nobody Can Brute-Force
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
Finding a faster way to multiply matrices means finding a short list of blocks that sum to the multiplication cube, and that list can be found neither by trying every list nor by always taking the move that looks best. Part 1 built the cube for matrices, a array with eight ones. Part 2 showed that blocks summing to are an algorithm with multiplications, and that Strassen’s method is a list of seven.

Finding an algorithm is the same job as emptying the cube

Part 2 handed us Strassen’s seven blocks without saying where they came from. Strassen found them by hand. Suppose nobody had, and we wanted them, or wanted a shorter list for bigger matrices. How would we look?

Move the blocks to the other side of the equation. If , then

Start with the cube, take away one block at a time, and try to be left with zeros in as few steps as possible. The AlphaTensor paper calls this TensorGame, and its rules take four lines (Fawzi et al. 2022):

  • The game starts from the tensor: “The start position of the game corresponds to the tensor representing the bilinear operation of interest”.
  • A move is three vectors , whose entries come from a small fixed set such as . The move subtracts their block: .
  • “The game ends when the state reaches the zero tensor”.
  • “For every step taken, we provide a reward of −1”, and a game that runs past a set number of moves is stopped with a further penalty.

There is one player and no opponent. The score is minus the number of moves, so playing well means finishing fast. By Part 2, a game won in moves is an algorithm with multiplications: winning the game in 7 moves is Strassen’s result, and winning the game in fewer than 49, in arithmetic modulo 2, was AlphaTensor’s.

The scene plays the game on the cube with entries , and . Three things to try, in order:

  1. Press Schoolbook’s next move eight times. The tile for nonzero cells left counts down 7, 6, 5 and on to 0. That is a win in 8 moves.
  2. Press Start over, then Strassen’s next move. The count goes up, from 8 to 12. Six more presses take it through 12, 12, 10, 8, 4 to 0: a win in 7.
  3. Press Start over and build a move by hand. Set in , in and in to . The tile for the count after this move reads 7 (−1), and Subtract this block plays it.

The second experiment is the strange one, and we come back to it. First, the obvious plan: the game is finite, so list every game and keep the shortest win.

Counting the games rules out trying them all

A move fills three vectors. For matrices a vector has entries, so a move is entries, and with allowed coefficients there are ways to fill them.

For the game with the five coefficients that is choices at one move. A Go player, on a board with 361 points, has at most 361. For matrices the count is , and for it is . With three coefficients in place of five, the game still has choices a move. The paper puts it as “more than actions for most interesting cases”, an action space “much larger than that of traditional board games such as chess and Go”.

A game is a sequence of moves, so the counts multiply. Seven moves of the game with five coefficients make sequences. A machine that wrote down a billion of them every second would need years. For matrices and 49 moves the number of sequences is about .

Those counts overstate the task. They include moves that subtract nothing, they count one block several times because flipping the signs of two of its vectors leaves it unchanged, and they count the same seven moves in all orders. So cut the game down as far as it will go. Allow only the entries , , . There are nonzero vectors, triples, and after removing the sign duplicates different blocks. Ignore order and ask how many sets of seven blocks there are: about . At a billion a second, checking them takes years, for the smallest case there is.

The calculator shows how fast the numbers leave the page. It opens on the game with five coefficients and seven moves. Choose and drag the slider to 49 moves: one move has choices, and the number of games has 1,644 digits.

Caveat: enumeration can be smarter than this

Nobody serious lists every sequence. A good exhaustive search prunes branches that cannot win and skips arrangements that are mirror images of ones already tried, and proofs can replace search: the case was closed in 1971, when Winograd proved that six multiplications are too few. The size of the space still bites one step up. The fewest multiplications for matrices is known only to lie between 19 and 23 (Bläser 2003; Laderman 1976), and the AlphaTensor paper says why: “the search space is so large that even the optimal algorithm for multiplying two 3 × 3 matrices is still unknown”.

Always taking the best-looking move finds eight, and never seven

If we cannot look at every game, we can try to play one game well. Matrices allow that. The singular value decomposition peels off the best rank-one layer of a matrix, then the best layer of what is left, and the result is the best possible approximation at every step (The Matrix That Rotates, Stretches, and Rotates Again). A greedy player gets the right answer.

Try the same plan on the cube. Measure a position by its number of nonzero cells, and always play the move that leaves the fewest. From the starting position there are 128,000 moves to compare, and the tally is lopsided: 8 of them lower the count, 176 leave it at 8, and 127,816 raise it, by as much as 56. The 8 that help are the 8 single cells of the cube. A greedy player takes one, faces the same choice with seven cells left, and takes another. It plays the schoolbook rule and wins in 8.

Strassen’s first move is among the 127,816. It takes the count from 8 to 12, as the second experiment showed, and the full run is 8, 12, 12, 12, 10, 8, 4, 0. The order of the seven moves does not rescue it. In every one of the 5,040 orders, the count climbs to 10 or more before it falls.

The scene makes the same point with one extra press. Start over, press Strassen’s next move, then press Greedy move. The count returns to 8 and the cube is back where it started: the best-looking reply to Strassen’s first move is to take it back. Left to finish from there, greedy needs 10 moves in all.

The seven-move win exists, and a player who insists on visible progress walks away from it at the first step. The game’s own score does not help either. Every move costs the same , whether it is Strassen’s first or a blunder, so the score says how long a finished game was and nothing about which unfinished position is promising. Nor is there a theorem to lean on in place of the singular value decomposition: finding the rank of a tensor is NP-hard (Håstad 1990), and the paper adds that it “is also hard in practice”.

Caveat: we tried one yardstick

Counting nonzero cells is one way to measure a position, and the result above belongs to that measure. Another measure might rank Strassen’s first move above a single cell. We know of no simple one that ranks the right moves first at every size. Learning such a measure from experience of the game is the job AlphaTensor gives to a neural network.

AlphaTensor learns the sense of progress that counting cannot give

AlphaTensor is built on AlphaZero, the system that learned Go and chess by playing itself, and it keeps AlphaZero’s two parts (Fawzi et al. 2022). Reinforcement Learning Splits on One Question has the background.

The first part is a network. It “takes as input a state (that is, a tensor to decompose), and outputs a policy and a value”: a ranking of promising moves, and an estimate of how many more moves the game will take. That estimate is the yardstick greedy lacked. The second part is a tree search that uses the network to look a few moves ahead along the lines it rates highly, in place of every one of the moves a position offers, and the games the search produces become training data for the network.

Two further ideas come from the problem itself. Taking a tensor apart is hard, but building one is easy: pick random blocks, add them up, and the result is a tensor with a known -move win. The paper trains on such made-up examples, which it calls synthetic demonstrations: “Although tensor decomposition is NP-hard, the inverse task of constructing the tensor from its rank-one factors is elementary.” And a multiplication cube can be written in other coordinates without changing the fewest moves it needs, so the system plays the same game in many disguises.

The results are counts of moves:

  • matrices in arithmetic modulo 2: 47 multiplications, against the 49 of Strassen’s method applied twice.
  • A matrix times a matrix: 76 multiplications, against the previous best of 80.
  • matrices in ordinary arithmetic: 49 multiplications, matching the record, reached by “more than 14,000 non-equivalent factorizations” where one was known before.

Matrix multiplication was a rule in Part 1 and a cube by the end of it. Part 2 showed that a list of blocks summing to the cube is an algorithm. Here the list became the record of a game, and the game showed why short lists are hard to find: the space is too wide to cover, and the short wins begin by making the position look worse. AlphaTensor did not make the space smaller. It learned which uphill moves are worth making. For matrices the fewest moves is still unknown.

Search. Too. Wide. Greedy. Finds. Eight. Seven. Climbs. First. Learn. Progress.

References

  • Fawzi, A., et al. (2022). Discovering faster matrix multiplication algorithms with reinforcement learning. Nature 610, 47–53.
  • Strassen, V. (1969). Gaussian elimination is not optimal. Numerische Mathematik 13, 354–356.
  • Winograd, S. (1971). On multiplication of 2 × 2 matrices. Linear Algebra and its Applications 4, 381–388.
  • Laderman, J. D. (1976). A noncommutative algorithm for multiplying 3 × 3 matrices using 23 multiplications. Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 82, 126–128.
  • Bläser, M. (2003). On the complexity of the multiplication of matrices of small formats. Journal of Complexity 19(1), 43–60.
  • Håstad, J. (1990). Tensor rank is NP-complete. Journal of Algorithms 11(4), 644–654.
  • The Matrix That Rotates, Stretches, and Rotates Again — rank-one layers of a matrix, where greedy works.
  • Reinforcement Learning Splits on One Question: Learn the Value, or Learn the Policy? — policies and values.
  • AlphaTensor, Part 1: Matrix Multiplication Is a Cube — the cube.
  • AlphaTensor, Part 2: A Factorization Is an Algorithm — why a list of blocks is an algorithm.

item.title: AlphaTensor, Part 2: A Factorization Is an Algorithm
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
A way of splitting the multiplication cube into simple blocks is a recipe for multiplying matrices with multiplications, and Strassen’s seven-multiplication method is a split into seven. Part 1 built the cube: a array of zeros and ones that records the rule for multiplying two matrices, with eight ones because the rule has eight products. Part 3 turns the search for a split into a game.

One multiplication can buy four products

Start with a piece of school algebra. The expression takes two additions and one multiplication to compute. Expand it and four products appear:

In Part 1 every product cost its own multiplication. Here one multiplication delivers four of them, bundled into one number.

The bundle is a mixed blessing. Two of the four, and , are products the rule wants: the first belongs in and the second in . The other two, and , appear nowhere in the product of two matrices. Add the bundle to both and and we have done some of the right work and some damage, and later steps have to undo the damage. Strassen’s method is seven bundles chosen so that all the damage cancels.

Cancelling looks like luck when it is written as algebra. On the cube it is geometry, so we go back to the cube.

A bundle is a block of the cube

The cube has one axis for the entries of , one for the entries of , and one for the entries of . A 1 in the cell means “the product goes into ”.

The bundle uses two entries of , namely and . It uses two entries of , and we add it to two entries of . So it puts a 1 in every cell whose three coordinates come from those three pairs: cells. Two of the eight are cells where the cube has a 1. The other six are the damage.

Three lists of weights describe the bundle. With the entries of a matrix taken in the order 11, 12, 21, 22:

The cell at position holds the product . An array built this way is written and called a rank-one tensor; CP or Tucker introduces it as the outer product of three vectors. We will call it a block. Weights may be negative: the sum has weights , and a cell holds when its three weights multiply to .

Read as an instruction, a block says three things:

  1. add up the entries of with the weights ;
  2. add up the entries of with the weights ;
  3. multiply the two sums, and add the result to the entries of with the weights .

Step 3 holds the only multiplication. A block costs one multiplication however many cells it covers.

If R blocks add up to the cube, R multiplications multiply the matrices

Suppose we find blocks whose sum, cell by cell, is the cube:

A sum of this shape is a CP factorization of . Tensor Factorizations and Tensor Inverses uses one to approximate data, with a sign. Here the sign is : every one of the 64 cells has to match.

Part 1 read the product off the cube with , where are the entries of read row by row. Put the factorization in place of and collect the sums:

That line changes the order of summation and does nothing else. It says the product can be computed in two stages:

The first stage does multiplications, one per block. The weights are fixed numbers, here , and , so applying them takes additions and subtractions and no multiplications of data by data. The number of blocks in the factorization is the number of multiplications in the algorithm. The AlphaTensor paper states it in one sentence: “A decomposition of into rank-one terms provides an algorithm for multiplying arbitrary matrices using scalar multiplications” (Fawzi et al. 2022).

The schoolbook rule is the split into eight single cells

The schoolbook rule fits this mould. Give , and one nonzero weight apiece and the block shrinks to one cell. Take , , : the block is the cell , and the instruction is “multiply by and add the result to ”.

The cube has eight ones, so this split has eight blocks and the schoolbook rule has eight multiplications. No block does any damage, and no block does more than one cell of work. To get under eight, some block has to cover more than one wanted cell, and the six-cells-of-damage problem returns.

Strassen’s seven blocks overshoot and cancel

Strassen published these seven products in 1969:

and the product is assembled from them with additions and subtractions:

Written as weights on the entries 11, 12, 21, 22 of each matrix, the seven blocks are:

product , weights on , weights on , weights on

The column is the assembly step read sideways: has weight on and on , and those are the two places appears in the formulas for .

One entry is short enough to check by hand. For :

The unwanted product arrives once with a minus sign from and once with a plus sign from . On the cube that is one cell, , going to and coming back to .

The scene adds the blocks one at a time. Press Add the next block once. Eight cells light up, the block of , and the tile counting cells that differ from the target goes from 8 to 12: two of the eight are wanted, six are damage, and six wanted cells are still missing. Keep pressing. The tile reads 12, 12, 10, 8, 4, and after the seventh block 0. Over the seven steps 20 different cells hold something; 12 of them end hollow, cancelled back to zero, and the 8 that are left are the cube. After the third block the cell in slice holds , and the fifth block clears it, as the algebra said. Switch to Schoolbook’s 8 for the contrast: every press fills one wanted cell and nothing is ever cancelled.

The same seven blocks run as an algorithm on numbers. With and , the example from Part 1, the seven products are and , and they assemble to , , and . Type other integers, or press Random matrices: the tile that compares the result with the schoolbook product stays at “yes”.

Seven beats eight because the entries can be matrices

On numbers, Strassen’s recipe is a bad trade. It uses 7 multiplications and 18 additions and subtractions where the schoolbook rule uses 8 and 4: 25 operations against 12.

The trade pays for a different reason. In every product the entries of stand on the left and the entries of on the right, and the recipe never swaps two factors. It never assumes . So the “entries” do not have to be numbers. They can be matrices.

Cut two matrices into quarters of size and treat the four quarters as the entries of a matrix. The recipe multiplies them with 7 products of quarters where the schoolbook rule needs 8. A product of two quarters is a smaller matrix multiplication, so apply the recipe to it again, and keep halving. After levels a matrix of size has cost multiplications of numbers under Strassen and under the schoolbook rule. Since and , the saving is in the exponent: in place of . The additions at every level cost in proportion to the number of entries, and the total work, additions included, still grows like (Strassen 1969).

size schoolbook, Strassen, multiplications saved
2 8 7 12.5%
8 512 343 33.0%
1,024 1,073,741,824 282,475,249 73.7%

Drag the slider to : the schoolbook rule does 3.80 multiplications for every one of Strassen’s.

One block fewer in the factorization of the cube lowers the exponent for matrices of every size. That is why the count of blocks is worth a search.

The fewest blocks has a name, and for 3 × 3 matrices nobody knows it

The smallest for which blocks sum to a tensor is the tensor’s rank. For the multiplication cube the rank is 7: Winograd proved in 1971 that six multiplications cannot do it.

For matrices the cube is with 27 ones, and its rank is an open problem. Laderman found a split into 23 blocks in 1976. The best proof says no split has fewer than 19 (Bläser 2003), and in arithmetic modulo 2 no fewer than 20 (Wang 2026). Where in that range the answer lies, nobody knows.

A fast algorithm for multiplying matrices and a short factorization of one fixed cube are the same object. “Invent a better algorithm” becomes “find fewer blocks that sum to ”: a search over short lists of small integers, which is a thing a machine can attempt. Part 3 measures how large that search is and shows how AlphaTensor plays it.

Blocks. Sum. Cube. Terms. Become. Multiplications. Seven. Beats. Eight. Recursively.

References

  • Strassen, V. (1969). Gaussian elimination is not optimal. Numerische Mathematik 13, 354–356.
  • Winograd, S. (1971). On multiplication of 2 × 2 matrices. Linear Algebra and its Applications 4, 381–388.
  • Laderman, J. D. (1976). A noncommutative algorithm for multiplying 3 × 3 matrices using 23 multiplications. Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 82, 126–128.
  • Bläser, M. (2003). On the complexity of the multiplication of matrices of small formats. Journal of Complexity 19(1), 43–60.
  • Wang, C. (2026). Automated lower bounds for bilinear complexity over finite fields. arXiv:2603.07280.
  • Fawzi, A., et al. (2022). Discovering faster matrix multiplication algorithms with reinforcement learning. Nature 610, 47–53.
  • CP or Tucker — rank-one tensors and the CP factorization.
  • Tensor Factorizations and Tensor Inverses — CP as an approximation of data.
  • AlphaTensor, Part 1: Matrix Multiplication Is a Cube — the cube and how to read the product off it.
  • AlphaTensor, Part 3: A Game Nobody Can Brute-Force — the search for a short factorization.

item.title: AlphaTensor, Part 1: Matrix Multiplication Is a Cube
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
The rule for multiplying two matrices fits in a block of zeros and ones, and the product can be read straight off that block. This is the first of three parts. Part 2 splits the block into pieces and gets a faster way to multiply; Part 3 shows how AlphaTensor turned the hunt for those pieces into a game for one player.

Eight multiplications look forced, and they are not

We learn to multiply matrices once and then stop looking at the rule. For two matrices it is

Count the work on the right: eight multiplications and four additions. With numbers,

Eight feels like a fact about the problem. The answer has four entries, every entry is a sum of two products, and all eight products are different. Where would a saving come from?

Yet in 1969 Volker Strassen multiplied matrices with seven multiplications. In 2022 a program from DeepMind called AlphaTensor found a way to multiply matrices in arithmetic modulo 2 with 47 multiplications, where the best known count had been 49, and the paper notes that this “improves on Strassen’s two-level algorithm for the first time, to our knowledge, since its discovery 50 years ago” (Fawzi et al. 2022).

Neither result comes from staring at the formula. Both come from treating “the rule for multiplying matrices” as an object that can be taken apart. This post builds the object.

Every product in the rule names an entry of A, an entry of B and a destination in C

Take one term of the rule, say in the top-left corner. Three facts pin it down: which entry of it uses, which entry of it uses, and which entry of it is added to. Here those are , and .

All eight terms fit that description, so the rule is a list of eight triples:

product entry of entry of added to

That table is matrix multiplication for matrices. It mentions no numbers. It works for every and every .

Put a 1 at each triple and the rule becomes a 4 × 4 × 4 cube

A list of triples is a set of points in a three-way grid. Give the grid one axis for the four entries of , one for the four entries of , and one for the four entries of . That makes cells. Put a 1 in the eight cells the table names and a 0 in the other 56.

To write this down we number the entries of a matrix by reading it row by row: , , , , and likewise for and . Then the array is

The second row of the table becomes : entry 2 of times entry 3 of goes to entry 1 of .

A grid of numbers with two axes is a matrix. A grid with three or more is a tensor, and is the matrix multiplication tensor for matrices. The AlphaTensor paper opens with this picture: “as , tensor entries located at and are set to 1” (Fawzi et al. 2022, Fig. 1).

We draw the cube as a stack of four trays, one per entry of , so that no cell hides behind another. Inside a tray the rows are the entries of and the columns are the entries of .

Press in the scene. The other trays pull away and fade, its two cubes stay lit, and the line under the buttons reads , which for the example matrices is . Then press the product : one cube grows, the scene labels it , and the example gives .

One formula reads the product off the cube

The cube is more than a record of the rule. It can do the multiplying. For every entry of the answer,

In words: to get entry of , look at tray , and for every cell on it multiply the entry of for its row by the entry of for its column by the number in the cell. Sixteen terms, of which fourteen are multiplied by 0 and vanish. On tray 1 the two cells that hold a 1 are and , so

A tray is a matrix of zeros and ones, and the formula is a sandwich with that matrix in the middle. Write and as columns, and for tray . Then , and for the first entry

Four trays, four sandwiches, four entries of . The tensor holds no data. The matrices and arrive as the two slices of bread.

Reading cell by cell costs one multiplication per 1

The formula tells us what the schoolbook rule costs. A cell that holds 0 contributes nothing and costs nothing. A cell that holds 1 costs one multiplication, times . The cube has eight ones, so reading it one cell at a time takes eight multiplications. The tile under the scene counts them.

The eight we started with is the number of ones in the cube. The count of multiplications in the schoolbook rule is a count of filled cells.

A bigger matrix gives a bigger, emptier cube

The construction works for any size. Two matrices have entries apiece, so the cube has cells along every side. The rule has one product for every choice of , and , so the cube holds ones.

matrices side of the cube cells ones share that is nonzero
4 64 8 12.5%
9 729 27 3.7%
16 4,096 64 1.6%
25 15,625 125 0.8%

Switch the scene to : nine trays, three cubes on every tray, and 27 multiplications if we read one cell at a time. The familiar “matrix multiplication takes multiplications” is the statement that the cube has ones and we pay for them one by one.

One multiplication per 1 is a choice

Reading the cube one cell at a time takes it apart into eight pieces, and every piece is one cell. Nothing in the formula says the pieces have to be cells. Part 2 takes the cube apart into seven pieces that overlap and cancel, shows that every piece still costs one multiplication, and so multiplies matrices with seven.

Rule. Becomes. Cube. Ones. Mark. Products. Count. Ones. Count. Multiplications.

References

  • Fawzi, A., et al. (2022). Discovering faster matrix multiplication algorithms with reinforcement learning. Nature 610, 47–53.
  • Strassen, V. (1969). Gaussian elimination is not optimal. Numerische Mathematik 13, 354–356.
  • AlphaTensor, Part 2: A Factorization Is an Algorithm — splitting the cube into blocks that cost one multiplication apiece.
  • AlphaTensor, Part 3: A Game Nobody Can Brute-Force — the search for a short split.

item.title: Collinearity, Part 2: Ridge, Principal Components, Lasso and Elastic Net
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
Every remedy for collinearity supplies, from outside the data, a value for the combination of coefficients the data cannot determine. The remedies differ in which value they supply and how firmly they hold it.

The remedies look like repairs. A regression with unstable coefficients goes into ridge, or the lasso, or a principal components step, and comes out with coefficients that hold still. The data did not change, so the information that was missing is still missing. The method filled the gap with an assumption, and the coefficients are stable because the assumption is.

Part 1 found the gap. With two nearly parallel predictor columns, the data fix the sum of the two coefficients and say almost nothing about their difference. With more columns the undetermined part is whichever combination nearly cancels.

  • What does each method assume about that combination?
  • What does the assumption cost when it is wrong?
  • Which problems does each method leave unsolved?
  • When is dropping a column, or doing nothing, the better choice?

1 The weak direction

The facts carried over from Part 1:

  • Write the singular value decomposition . Least squares is .
  • Near collinearity is a small . Its is the weak direction: a combination of coefficients that barely changes the fitted values.
  • Dividing by the small turns noise in into large swings of along .
  • For two standardised columns at correlation , the weak direction is : raise one coefficient, lower the other.

1.1 The synthetic data

The two scenes reuse Part 1’s synthetic data with one change.

  • Rows. , the same values and the same 200 noise draws as Part 1.
  • Predictors. Two centred columns with standard deviation 1 and correlation .
  • Target. , noise standard deviation 0.6. Part 1 used .
  • Why the change. With true coefficients the true difference is zero, and a method that pushes the difference towards zero would look free. With the difference is , and pushing it towards zero is an error the scenes can show.
  • What it stands in for. Two measurements that track each other and matter unequally.

2 One formula for the linear remedies

Standardise the columns and write the loss as the mean squared error, . Let , the eigenvalues of . Ridge and principal components regression both return

least squares with each term multiplied by a filter factor between 0 and 1.

The lasso and the elastic net are not of this form. They act on the coefficients themselves and can set them to zero.

3 What each method minimises

Every method here minimises , or the MSE under a restriction. The scene draws that objective for two predictors.

With least squares at 0.99 it is Part 1’s trough. The answers of the 200 samples lie strewn along its floor, the coefficient has a standard deviation of 0.68, and a typical answer is 0.96 away from the truth.

3.1 Ridge

Ridge (Hoerl and Kennard, 1970) adds the squared length of the coefficient vector:

  • In the trough. The penalty adds curvature in every direction. Across the trough that is negligible beside the curvature already there. Along the floor it is most of what there is.
  • Filter factors. For two columns, and . At and : and . The sum of the coefficients keeps 95% of its least-squares value and the difference keeps 9%.
  • Condition number. That of is : 19 in place of 199.
  • As extra rows. Ridge is least squares on the data plus one made-up row per predictor, in which that predictor alone is non-zero and the response is 0. Those are rows in which the predictors move separately, the kind the data lacked.
  • As a prior. It is the posterior mode under independent Gaussian priors centred on zero.
  1. Press ridge and set the penalty weight to 0.10. The floor of the trough has curled up into a bowl. The pink dot, least squares for this sample at , has been pulled along the floor to the amber answer at .
  2. Read the stats. The standard deviation of the coefficient is 0.07. The average answer is , and the truth is .
  3. Slide the weight down to 0.018. The average answer moves to and the typical distance from the truth is 0.57, the lowest ridge reaches at this correlation.
  4. Slide it up to 1.0. Both coefficients shrink towards zero together, to an average of , and the distance rises to 0.85.

Ridge does not find the difference. It replaces “unknown” with “close to zero”, which here is wrong by 1.

3.2 Principal components regression

Principal components regression (PCR) rotates the predictors onto their principal components, the directions , regresses on the first of them, and rotates back.

  • For two columns. The first component is the average of the two predictors and the second is their difference. Keeping one component forces .
  • Filter factors. 1 for the kept components, 0 for the others: ridge’s shrinkage taken to its limit for the small and switched off for the large ones.
  • What is. The tuning knob, in whole steps.
  1. Press one component. The amber line on the surface is the restriction , and every answer lies on it.
  2. Read the stats. The standard deviation of the coefficient is 0.05, the average answer is , and the typical distance from the truth is 0.71.
  3. Press 0.9. Least squares has a typical distance of 0.31 at this correlation. One component still has 0.71.

That 0.71 is the length of the part of the truth that lies along the weak direction: , and . PCR deletes that part at every correlation. At deleting it costs less than estimating it. At it costs more.

PCR chooses components by the variance of the predictors and never looks at . A low-variance component can be the one that predicts (Jolliffe, 1982).

3.3 Lasso

The lasso (Tibshirani, 1996) penalises the sum of absolute values:

  • What it is for. The absolute value has a corner at zero, so the minimum often sits exactly on . The lasso selects predictors.
  • On the floor of the trough. Along the floor is fixed. While both coefficients are positive, is that same sum, so the penalty is flat along the floor. The lasso adds no curvature where curvature was missing.
  • What breaks the tie. The slight tilt of the floor in each sample: noise.
  1. Press 0.99, lasso, and set the weight to 0.10. The two dark lines on the surface are and . The grey answers are still spread along the floor, and some have stopped on a line.
  2. Read the stats. The standard deviation of the coefficient is 0.54, against 0.68 for least squares. 4 samples drop and 54 drop .
  3. Press New noise three times. The answer goes from to , and .
  4. Press 0.999. 48 samples drop , the predictor with three times the true coefficient, and 82 drop .

With collinear predictors the lasso still selects, and the selection is unstable. It reports one predictor of a pair as irrelevant, and a different sample reverses the report.

3.4 Elastic net

The elastic net (Zou and Hastie, 2005) uses both penalties. The scene uses equal weights:

  • The squared term curls the floor of the trough, as ridge does, so correlated predictors share the weight. Zou and Hastie call this the grouping effect.
  • The absolute term keeps the corner at zero, so predictors unrelated to can still be dropped.
  1. Press 0.99, elastic net, weight 0.10. The answers have gathered: the standard deviation of the coefficient is 0.12, and no sample drops either predictor.
  2. Press 0.999. Still none dropped, against 130 of 200 for the lasso at the same weight.
  3. Read the average answer, . It shares the weight equally. The truth does not.

3.5 Summary of the scene

Least squares is right on average and far off in any one sample. Ridge, one component and the elastic net are wrong on average by a fixed amount and stay close to that answer in every sample. The lasso keeps most of the spread.

4 The cost

The stability is bought with bias, and the bias sits where Part 1 located the damage: at points where the predictors disagree.

  1. Start with least squares at 0.99. At the true value is 1.50. The average prediction is 1.52, its standard deviation is 2.05, and the typical error is 2.04.
  2. Press ridge, weight 0.10. The fan closes. The average prediction is 0.14 with a standard deviation of 0.19, and the typical error is 1.37. Every plane now misses the dark dot, and all miss it by about the same amount.
  3. Press one component. The prediction at is 0.00 in every sample. The typical error is 1.50, the true value itself.
  4. Compare at , where the predictors agree. The typical error is 0.14 for least squares, 0.20 for ridge at 0.10, and 0.14 for one component.
  5. Press 0.999 and least squares. The typical error at is 6.47. For ridge at 0.10 it is 1.49.
  • A point where the predictors disagree is a point along the weak direction. Least squares answers there with a guess that is right on average and wild in any one sample. The remedies answer with the assumption: no effect of the difference.
  • Whether the trade is good depends on how wild the guess was. At an error of 1.5 replaces one of 6.5. At ridge at 0.10 has a typical error of 0.82 there and least squares 0.64.
  • No method predicts well where the predictors disagree. The training rows hold no evidence about such points, and a penalty adds none.

5 Real data

5.1 The diabetes data

  • Source. Efron, Hastie, Johnstone and Tibshirani (2004), shipped with scikit-learn: 442 diabetes patients, ten baseline measurements, and a measure of disease progression a year later.
  • What Part 1 found. Total cholesterol (s1), LDL (s2), HDL (s3) and the triglyceride column (s5) are tied by the Friedewald formula, from which LDL is computed. The variance inflation factor (VIF) of total cholesterol is 59, and its least-squares coefficient is negative with a standard error half its size.
  • What this post asks of it. What each remedy does to those coefficients, and whether any remedy predicts better.
  • Cost of a wrong answer. Reporting a stabilised coefficient as an effect, or reporting a selected predictor as the relevant one.
  • Why these methods fit. Ten standardised predictors, one strong dependence among four of them, and enough rows to resample.

5.1.1 Filter factors

Code 
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.4, 2.8), sharey=True)
idx = np.arange(1, p + 1)
w = 0.38
axes[0].bar(idx - w / 2, d_eig / (d_eig + lam_cv), w, color=PURPLE, label=f"λ = {lam_cv:.4f} (cross-validated)")
axes[0].bar(idx + w / 2, d_eig / (d_eig + 20 * lam_cv), w, color=TEAL, label=f"λ = {20 * lam_cv:.3f}")
axes[0].set_title("Ridge")
axes[0].legend(frameon=True, framealpha=0.92, edgecolor=RULE, fontsize=7.5, loc="lower left")
axes[1].bar(idx, (idx <= k_best).astype(float), 0.6, color=AMBER)
axes[1].set_title(f"Principal components, k = {k_best}")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xticks(idx)
    ax.set_xlabel("singular direction")
axes[0].set_ylabel("filter factor")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
  • The eigenvalues run from 4.02 down to 0.078 and 0.0086. The last is the Friedewald identity.
  • Cross-validation chooses a ridge weight of 0.0039, which leaves the weakest direction with a factor of 0.69. Prediction error does not ask for more.
  • Of the ten possible settings, PCR with 7 components has the lowest cross-validated error. It deletes the 3 weakest directions.

5.1.2 Coefficient paths

Code 
lams = np.logspace(-4, 1, 80)
ridge_path = np.array([np.linalg.solve(G + lam * np.eye(p), Z.T @ yc / n) for lam in lams])
# scikit-learn's lasso minimises RSS/(2n) + alpha |b|_1, so lambda = 2 alpha here; its elastic
# net with l1_ratio rho minimises RSS/(2n) + alpha rho |b|_1 + alpha (1 - rho) |b|^2 / 2, so
# this post's equal mix lambda (|b|_1 / 2 + |b|^2 / 2) is alpha = 0.75 lambda, rho = 1/3.
_, lasso_coefs, _ = lasso_path(Z, yc, alphas=lams[::-1] / 2)
_, enet_coefs, _ = enet_path(Z, yc, alphas=0.75 * lams[::-1], l1_ratio=1 / 3)
lasso_cv = LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=0).fit(Z, y)
enet_cv = ElasticNetCV(l1_ratio=1 / 3, cv=5, random_state=0).fit(Z, y)
chosen = {"Ridge": lam_cv, "Lasso": 2 * lasso_cv.alpha_, "Elastic net": enet_cv.alpha_ / 0.75}
paths = {"Ridge": ridge_path, "Lasso": lasso_coefs.T[::-1], "Elastic net": enet_coefs.T[::-1]}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7.6, 2.9), sharey=True)
for ax, (name, path) in zip(axes, paths.items()):
    for j, c in enumerate(names):
        if c not in ("s1", "s2"):
            ax.plot(lams, path[:, j], color=RULE, lw=1)
    ax.plot(lams, path[:, names.index("s1")], color=PURPLE, lw=1.8, label="total cholesterol (s1)")
    ax.plot(lams, path[:, names.index("s2")], color=AMBER, lw=1.8, label="LDL (s2)")
    ax.axvline(chosen[name], color=MUTED, lw=0.7, ls="--")
    ax.axhline(0, color=MUTED, lw=0.5)
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_title(name)
    ax.set_xlabel("penalty weight λ")
axes[0].set_ylabel("coefficient")
axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=7.5, loc="lower right")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
  • Ridge. Between and the coefficient of total cholesterol goes from -37.3 to -6.3 and LDL’s from +22.3 to -1.9. Body mass index goes from 24.7 to 24.1. A small weight removes the opposed pair and leaves the predictors outside the dependence alone.
  • Lasso. The pair holds its opposed values until is near 0.1. LDL then falls to zero at 0.54, and total cholesterol keeps a negative coefficient after it.
  • Elastic net. The ridge shape, at larger weights because half of the weight goes to the absolute-value term.
  • The dashed lines. For ridge and the lasso, cross-validation stops short of the weight at which the pair settles. For the elastic net it does not: at its chosen weight the coefficients are -4.2 and -3.2.

5.1.3 Stability and prediction

Two measurements for each method, with its tuning chosen by cross-validation:

  • Stability. Refit on 500 bootstrap resamples of the 442 patients and record the coefficient of total cholesterol.
  • Prediction. Ten-fold cross-validated root mean squared error, repeated ten times.

“Drop LDL” is least squares on the nine predictors that remain when the computed column is removed.

Code 
keep_no_ldl = [j for j, c in enumerate(names) if c != "s2"]


class DropLDL(LinearRegression):
    def fit(self, X, y):
        return super().fit(X[:, keep_no_ldl], y)

    def predict(self, X):
        return super().predict(X[:, keep_no_ldl])


def s1_coef(model, name):
    if name == "PCR, 7 components":
        return (model[1].components_.T @ model[2].coef_)[i1]
    if name == "Drop LDL":
        return model[-1].coef_[keep_no_ldl.index(i1)]
    return model[-1].coef_[i1]


models = {
    "Least squares": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LinearRegression()),
    "Ridge": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), RidgeCV(alphas=ALPHAS)),
    "PCR, 7 components": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), PCA(n_components=k_best), LinearRegression()),
    "Lasso": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=0)),
    "Elastic net": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), ElasticNetCV(l1_ratio=1 / 3, cv=5, random_state=0)),
    "Drop LDL": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), DropLDL()),
}
B = 500
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
resamples = [rng.integers(0, n, n) for _ in range(B)]
boot = {name: np.array([s1_coef(m.fit(X_raw[ix], y[ix]), name) for ix in resamples]) for name, m in models.items()}
cv_rmse = {}
for name, m in models.items():
    mse = -cross_val_score(m, X_raw, y, cv=cv10, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error")
    cv_rmse[name] = np.sqrt(mse.reshape(10, 10).mean(1))
rows = []
for name in models:
    b = boot[name]
    rows.append(
        {
            "Method": name,
            "Mean": f"{b.mean():.1f}",
            "sd": f"{b.std():.1f}",
            "Positive": f"{(b > 0).mean():.0%}",
            "Exactly zero": f"{(b == 0).mean():.0%}",
            "CV error": f"{cv_rmse[name].mean():.1f} [{cv_rmse[name].min():.1f}, {cv_rmse[name].max():.1f}]",
        }
    )
md(pd.DataFrame(rows), index=False, colalign=("left",) + ("right",) * 5)
  • Prediction. The methods are within 0.3 of each other, 54.7 to 55.0, on a response whose standard deviation is 77. With 442 rows whose predictors follow the training pattern, collinearity was not costing any prediction accuracy, so no remedy could buy any.
  • Ridge and lasso. Tuned for prediction, both leave the coefficient as unstable as least squares: a standard deviation of 21.6 and 20.1 against 18.4. Cross-validation picks the weight that predicts best, and prediction did not need the pair settled.
  • Elastic net and PCR. These settle it: 2.2 and 1.6.
  • Drop LDL. One deleted column gives a standard deviation of 5.4 at the same prediction error.

The stable answers disagree with each other about the size of the coefficient. Each reflects its method’s assumption about the weak direction, and the data cannot rank the assumptions.

5.1.4 Fewer rows

Remedies do improve prediction when rows are scarce, because then the noise in the weak directions reaches the predictions.

Code 
def pcr_cv(Xtr, ytr, Xte):
    best, best_k = np.inf, 1
    for k in range(1, min(p, len(ytr) - 6) + 1):
        model = make_pipeline(PCA(n_components=k), LinearRegression())
        score = -cross_val_score(model, Xtr, ytr, cv=5, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error").mean()
        if score < best:
            best, best_k = score, k
    return make_pipeline(PCA(n_components=best_k), LinearRegression()).fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte)


sizes = [20, 30, 50, 100, 200]
small = {s: {k: [] for k in ["Least squares", "Ridge", "PCR", "Lasso", "Elastic net"]} for s in sizes}
for size in sizes:
    for seed in range(200):
        perm = np.random.default_rng(seed).permutation(n)
        tr, te = perm[:size], perm[size:]
        sc = StandardScaler().fit(X_raw[tr])
        Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = sc.transform(X_raw[tr]), sc.transform(X_raw[te]), y[tr], y[te]
        preds = {
            "Least squares": LinearRegression().fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte),
            "Ridge": RidgeCV(alphas=ALPHAS).fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte),
            "PCR": pcr_cv(Xtr, ytr, Xte),
            "Lasso": LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=0, max_iter=5000).fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte),
            "Elastic net": ElasticNetCV(l1_ratio=1 / 3, cv=5, random_state=0, max_iter=5000).fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte),
        }
        for k, pr in preds.items():
            small[size][k].append(np.sqrt(np.mean((pr - yte) ** 2)))
rows = []
for size in sizes:
    row = {"Training rows": str(size)}
    for k, v in small[size].items():
        lo, mid, hi = np.percentile(v, [5, 50, 95])
        row[k] = f"{mid:.1f} [{lo:.1f}, {hi:.1f}]"
    rows.append(row)
md(pd.DataFrame(rows), index=False, colalign=("right",) * 6)
  • With 20 training rows least squares has a median error of 85.9 and ridge 63.2.
  • With 50 the gap is 61.3 against 58.3.
  • With 200 all five methods are within 0.2.

5.2 Longley: the two columns

  • Source. Longley (1967), shipped with statsmodels: 16 annual observations of the US economy, 1947 to 1962.
  • What Part 1 found. Total employment regressed on standardised GNP and population gives coefficients of 6,279 and −2,850, although each predictor alone has a coefficient near 3,400. The two columns correlate at 0.991.
  • What this post asks of it. What a ridge penalty does to that pair.
  • Cost of a wrong answer. Reading the negative coefficient, or the stabilised one, as the effect of population.
  • Why it fits. Two columns, so the sum and the difference can be read off.
Code 
Lg = sm.datasets.longley.load_pandas().data
Z2 = ((Lg[["GNP", "POP"]] - Lg[["GNP", "POP"]].mean()) / Lg[["GNP", "POP"]].std()).values
yL = Lg["TOTEMP"].values - Lg["TOTEMP"].mean()
m = len(yL) - 1  # the sample standard deviation divides by n - 1, as in Part 1
G2 = Z2.T @ Z2 / m
rows, longley = [], {}
for lam in [0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.032, 0.1]:
    b = np.linalg.solve(G2 + lam * np.eye(2), Z2.T @ yL / m)
    longley[lam] = b
    rows.append({"$\\lambda$": f"{lam:g}", "GNP": f"{b[0]:,.0f}", "Population": f"{b[1]:,.0f}", "Sum": f"{b.sum():,.0f}", "Difference": f"{b[0] - b[1]:,.0f}"})
md(pd.DataFrame(rows), index=False, colalign=("right",) * 5)
  • The sum moves from 3,429 to 3,265 from the first row to the last.
  • The difference falls from 9,129 to 747.
  • Population’s coefficient turns positive between and .

The sign of population’s coefficient is set by the penalty weight. Sixteen yearly figures in which GNP and population rose together cannot say what population does at fixed GNP, with a penalty or without one.

6 Other approaches

  • Drop a column. When one column is computed from others, as LDL is, remove it. On the diabetes data that took the standard deviation of total cholesterol’s coefficient from 18.4 to 5.4 at no cost in prediction. The coefficient that remains then describes that predictor with the dropped one free to vary alongside it.
  • Combine columns. Replace a group by one index: an average, a ratio, a sum. This is PCR with the components chosen by subject knowledge.
  • Collect rows that break the pattern. A designed experiment sets the predictors independently, and is the only item on this list that adds information about the weak direction.
  • Partial least squares. Like PCR, but each component is chosen for its covariance with , which answers Jolliffe’s objection.
  • An informative prior. Ridge is a prior centred on zero. A prior centred on a value from earlier studies puts outside knowledge into the weak direction explicitly.
  • Centre before forming powers and products. and are nearly collinear when is far from zero: for 50 evenly spaced values from 10 to 20 their correlation is 0.996, and after centring it is 0.000. The fitted curve is the same either way. Centring changes which coefficients are asked for.
  • Errors in the predictors. Part 1 showed that noise in is amplified by when the residual is large. Total least squares models that noise; none of the penalties here do.
  • Nothing. For predicting new rows that follow the training pattern, with enough rows, least squares on collinear predictors is already as accurate as any remedy.

7 Choosing

A weight chosen for prediction and a weight chosen for stable coefficients are different weights. On the diabetes data cross-validation chose the first and left the coefficients unsettled.

Remedies. Assume. Ridge. Shrinks. Components. Delete. Lasso. Flips. Nets. Share. None. Recovers.

8 References

  • Efron, B., Hastie, T., Johnstone, I., and Tibshirani, R. (2004). Least angle regression. Annals of Statistics, 32(2), 407–499.
  • Hoerl, A. E., and Kennard, R. W. (1970). Ridge regression: biased estimation for nonorthogonal problems. Technometrics, 12(1), 55–67.
  • Jolliffe, I. T. (1982). A note on the use of principal components in regression. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series C, 31(3), 300–303.
  • Longley, J. W. (1967). An appraisal of least squares programs for the electronic computer from the point of view of the user. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 62(319), 819–841.
  • Tibshirani, R. (1996). Regression shrinkage and selection via the lasso. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 58(1), 267–288.
  • Zou, H., and Hastie, T. (2005). Regularization and variable selection via the elastic net. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 67(2), 301–320.
  • Collinearity, Part 1: The Direction the Data Cannot See.

item.title: Collinearity, Part 1: The Direction the Data Cannot See
item.dc:creator: Ravi Kalia
item.description:
When two predictors carry nearly the same information, least squares still predicts well, but it can no longer say how much each predictor contributes: the individual coefficients swing with every small change to the data.

The symptom is familiar. A regression is refitted with one more month of data. Its predictions barely move and its is the same to three decimals, yet one coefficient has doubled and another has changed sign. The software is working. The data pin down some combinations of the coefficients tightly and others hardly at all, and a nearly collinear pair of columns is the smallest example of the second kind.

The questions came from one scene in an interactive linear-algebra stage. A button there moves a target vector by 2%, and with the two predictor columns half a degree apart the fitted coefficients go from to .

  • 2% of what?
  • Why is the response violent only when the columns are nearly parallel?
  • Do the fitted values and the loss move as well?
  • Is a change to the predictors worse than a change to the target?
  • What changes with more than two columns, and with real data?

Part 2 covers what to do about it: ridge, principal components, the lasso, and the elastic net.

1 The symptom

The first scene uses synthetic data, so the cause can be turned up and down.

  • Rows. .
  • Predictors. Two columns , centred, with standard deviation 1 and correlation .
  • Target. , with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.6.
  • What it stands in for. Any pair of measurements that track each other: two assays of the same quantity, a country’s output and its population, total and LDL cholesterol.

Changing turns towards and leaves the noise, the true coefficients , and the 40 values of as they were.

Each sheet is one least-squares plane , fitted to the same values under a different draw of the noise.

  1. Press r = 0. The grey shadows of the data fill the floor, the 25 planes lie almost on top of each other, and the coefficient has a standard deviation of 0.09 over 200 noise draws.
  2. Press 0.99. The shadows collapse onto a narrow band along the diagonal. The planes still agree above that band and fan out away from it, as if hinged on a fence that runs over the data. The standard deviation of the coefficient is 0.68.
  3. Read the sum. The standard deviation of is 0.09, lower than the 0.13 it had at .
  4. Compare the two vertical lines. At , a point like the data, the predictions have standard deviation 0.14. At , where the predictors disagree, it is 2.05.
  5. Press 0.999, then New noise four times. The amber points barely move, and the solid plane’s coefficients go from to , , and . Both true values are 1.

The planes pivot because the data say where the plane is along the fence and almost nothing about its tilt across it.

2 Notation

  • , the predictor columns, centred and of equal length.
  • , the target.
  • , the least-squares coefficients, and , the fitted vector.
  • , the angle between and as vectors in . For centred columns , the sample correlation.

Collinear means : one column is a multiple of the other, is singular, and no unique exists. Nearly collinear means is small.

Correlation compresses the scale near 1.

3 Which 2%

With observations, , and are three arrows in , and least squares is a projection.

  • The columns span a plane. is the point of that plane closest to : its shadow.
  • The coefficients are the coordinates of in the basis : go steps along , then steps along .
  • The residual is perpendicular to the plane, and its squared length is the minimum loss.

With the picture fits on a screen. The scene uses , and , a synthetic target chosen so that at every angle before any nudge.

The three buttons add a vector with to . That is the 2%: a change in the target of 2% of its own length. Its direction decides what happens.

  1. Press 0.99, then out of the floor. The coefficients do not move. The squared residual grows by 9.1%.
  2. Press along the columns. moves by 2.2% of its length and the coefficients by 1.6%.
  3. Press across them. moves by the same 2.2%. The coefficients move by 22%.
  4. Keep across them and press 0.999, then θ = 0.5°. The change in the coefficients is 71%, then 362%: from to . The route to now runs 2.19 units backwards along and 3.59 units forwards along to land 0.03 from where it started.

The fitted vector is never the unstable part. Its coordinates in a basis of two nearly parallel arrows are.

4 The linear algebra

4.1 Sum and difference

Take the columns to have length 1. Their Gram matrix and its eigenvectors are

with eigenvalues and . The singular values of are their square roots:

  • has length , between 1 and . Raising both coefficients together moves the fitted vector a long way.
  • has length . Raising one coefficient and lowering the other by the same amount moves the fitted vector by almost nothing, because the two columns nearly cancel.

is the direction the data cannot see. A unit step along it changes every fitted value by a total length of , so the data hold almost no evidence for or against that step.

4.2 Least squares in the singular basis

Write the singular value decomposition , with the unit vectors along and . Then

  • sets the sum .
  • sets the difference .
  • A nudge changes the coefficients by . The part of along is divided by .

That accounts for the scene.

  • The target has length 1.565, so the nudge has length 0.0313.
  • At the smaller singular value is 0.00617.
  • A nudge along moves the coefficients by 0.0313 ÷ 0.00617 = 5.07, which is 362% of .
  • The same nudge along moves them by 0.0221.

The scene that prompted the questions uses a nudge perpendicular to , which lies almost entirely along at small angles, and a target with : the same division, giving 324% at half a degree.

4.3 Many noise draws

Random noise has a component along in every sample, so repeated samples scatter the coefficients along .

Code 
n, sigma, beta_true = 40, 0.6, np.array([1.0, 1.0])


def pair(theta_deg, n, rng):
    """Two centred unit-length columns at angle theta."""
    Z = rng.standard_normal((n, 2))
    Z -= Z.mean(0)
    Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(Z)
    t = np.deg2rad(theta_deg)
    return np.column_stack([Q[:, 0], np.cos(t) * Q[:, 0] + np.sin(t) * Q[:, 1]])

5 The condition number

5.1 Definition and the two-column value

The condition number of is the ratio of its largest to its smallest singular value, . It measures how unequally stretches different directions.

For two columns of equal length,

  • stays between 1 and whatever the angle: two unit columns cannot add up to more than a vector of length 2.
  • goes to zero in proportion to .
  • So grows like . Halving the angle doubles it. Nothing is special about any threshold; the ratio is unbounded because its denominator reaches zero when the columns coincide.

5.2 What it bounds

For a nudge to that lies in the column plane,

  • The bound is reached when lies along and along : the fit uses the strong direction and the nudge hits the weak one.
  • The denominator is , not . A target that is mostly residual has a small fitted vector, and the same nudge is a larger fraction of it.
  • is a worst case. The nudge along the columns in the scene is nowhere near it.

is also the distance, in the spectral norm, from to the nearest matrix with exactly collinear columns (the Eckart–Young theorem). Relative to that distance is . At a 1% change to is enough to make the columns exactly dependent.

5.3 A change to X or a change to y

The target enters linearly, so a nudge to is amplified by at most . The predictors enter through the pseudoinverse , and the first-order bound for a perturbation of has two terms (Wedin, 1973; Golub and Van Loan, 2013, §5.3):

where is the angle between and the column plane, so .

  • With an exact fit, and a change to is no worse than a change to .
  • With a residual, the term appears. Perturbing tilts the plane, and the residual, which was perpendicular to the old plane, acquires a component inside the new one along the weak direction.

A simulation separates the two cases. It is synthetic: , unit columns at angle , plus a residual perpendicular to both columns, scaled to 0%, 5% or 30% of the signal’s length. Each of 1,000 seeds applies one random perturbation of relative size 2% to , and separately to .

Code 
def one_seed(theta, resid, seed):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n = 50
    X = pair(theta, n, rng)
    signal = X @ np.array([1.0, 1.0])
    e = rng.standard_normal(n)
    e -= X @ np.linalg.lstsq(X, e, rcond=None)[0]
    y = signal + resid * np.linalg.norm(signal) * e / np.linalg.norm(e)
    b0 = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]
    dy = rng.standard_normal(n)
    dy *= 0.02 * np.linalg.norm(y) / np.linalg.norm(dy)
    dX = rng.standard_normal((n, 2))
    dX *= 0.02 * np.linalg.norm(X, 2) / np.linalg.norm(dX, 2)
    by = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y + dy, rcond=None)[0]
    bx = np.linalg.lstsq(X + dX, y, rcond=None)[0]
    return np.linalg.norm(by - b0) / np.linalg.norm(b0), np.linalg.norm(bx - b0) / np.linalg.norm(b0)


def cell(v):
    lo, mid, hi = np.percentile(v, [5, 50, 95]) * 100
    return f"{mid:.1f}% [{lo:.1f}, {hi:.1f}]"


xy = {}
rows = []
for r in [0.0, 0.99, 0.999, 0.99996]:
    theta = np.degrees(np.arccos(r)) if r < 0.9999 else 0.5
    row = {"$\\theta$": f"{theta:.2f}°", "$\\kappa$": f"{1 / np.tan(np.deg2rad(theta) / 2):.1f}"}
    for resid in [0.0, 0.05, 0.30]:
        out = np.array([one_seed(theta, resid, s) for s in range(1000)])
        xy[(r, resid)] = np.median(out, axis=0) * 100
        if resid == 0.0:
            row["nudge $y$"] = cell(out[:, 0])
        row[f"nudge $X$, residual {resid:.0%}"] = cell(out[:, 1])
    rows.append(row)

  • A random nudge to is amplified in proportion to , at about a tenth of the worst case, because a random direction in 50 dimensions has only a small component along .
  • With an exact fit, the same-sized change to does less than the change to : 9% against 42% at half a degree.
  • With a residual 30% as long as the signal, the change to does more: 148% against 42%.

Regression data have residuals, so in practice noise in the predictors is the more damaging of the two. The reason is the size of the residual, and the claim fails for a system that is solved exactly.

5.4 Floating point

Rounding in the arithmetic is one more perturbation, of relative size about in double precision, and amplifies it as it does any other.

  • A solver that works on directly (QR or the SVD) loses about of its 16 digits.
  • The normal equations work on , whose condition number is , and lose twice as many.
Code 
rows = []
for k in [1e2, 1e4, 1e6, 1e8]:
    theta = np.degrees(2 * np.arctan(1 / k))
    err_ne, err_ls = [], []
    for s in range(200):
